title: Hurricane - Preparation and Survival
summary: Get your household through a hurricane: know your surge zone, leave early when told, shelter correctly if you stay, and avoid the after-storm hazards that kill more people than the wind.

steps.title: Know your zone and your risk before the season
steps.body: Look up your hurricane evacuation zone with your county or state emergency management office, and check your storm surge risk on the National Hurricane Center's national storm surge maps. Check your flood risk on the FEMA Flood Map Service Center too. Water - storm surge and inland rain flooding - causes most hurricane deaths, so the question is 'Could water reach my home?' before 'How strong is the wind?' Standard homeowner's policies usually do not cover flooding. Flood insurance through the NFIP normally takes 30 days to start, so buy it months ahead, not when a storm forms. Write down where you would go if told to leave: a friend or relative inland, a hotel outside the zone, or a public shelter. Plan your route and a backup route.

steps.title: Build your kit and protect the house early
steps.body: Stock several days of food and water (1 gallon (3.8 L) per person per day), medicines, pet supplies, cash, flashlights, a battery or hand-crank NOAA Weather Radio, chargers, and a first aid kit. Put important papers in a waterproof container and keep password-protected digital copies. Install hurricane shutters or have pre-cut plywood (marked for each window) ready. Do not tape windows - tape does not stop glass from breaking. Clear gutters and drains, trim weak limbs, and plan where outdoor furniture, grills, and trash cans will go. Choose your high-wind shelter spot: a FEMA safe room, an ICC 500 storm shelter, or a small interior windowless room on the lowest floor that will not flood.

steps.title: Track the storm and act on watches and warnings
steps.body: Follow the National Hurricane Center and your local NWS office. A Hurricane Watch means hurricane conditions are possible, usually about 48 hours out. A Hurricane Warning means they are expected, usually about 36 hours out. Storm Surge Watches and Warnings are separate - take them just as seriously. Since 2025 NHC can issue advisories up to 72 hours before winds or surge arrive, and for 2026 the forecast cone graphic also shows inland watches and warnings. Remember the cone shows where the center may go, not the size of the storm: damage and flooding often reach far outside it. At the Watch stage, fuel the car, get cash, refill prescriptions, charge batteries, and secure the yard.

steps.title: Evacuate early when told - or sooner
steps.body: If officials order your zone to evacuate, leave right away. If you live in a mobile or manufactured home, an RV, or any temporary structure, plan to leave for any hurricane - they are not safe in hurricane winds even outside a surge zone. Many people choose to leave before an order if they have medical needs, small children, pets, or a long drive, because traffic and fuel shortages build fast. Take your kit, documents, and medicines. Follow official routes and never drive around barricades. A common rule from emergency managers: run from the water, hide from the wind. You only need to go tens of miles, not hundreds - far enough to get out of the surge and flood zone into a sturdy building.

steps.title: If you stay, shelter in the right place
steps.body: Stay indoors and away from windows and glass doors. With no flooding, go to your safe room or the interior windowless room on the lowest level that will not flood. If water starts coming in, move to the highest floor. Do not go into a closed attic - people have been trapped and drowned there as water rose. Only go onto the roof if you must, and signal for help. Keep the radio on. Do not go outside when the wind suddenly calms: you may be in the eye, and the other side of the eyewall will hit with full force from the opposite direction, sometimes within minutes. Do not drive during the storm - wind can roll vehicles and bridges may wash out.

steps.title: Stay out of floodwater
steps.body: Turn around, don't drown. Six inches (15 cm) of fast-moving water can knock an adult down, and about 1 foot (30 cm) can float or sweep away a car. You cannot see if the road under the water is still there, especially at night. Floodwater also carries sewage, chemicals, sharp debris, snakes, and can be electrified by downed lines. Do not walk, swim, wade, or drive through it. Inland rain flooding can last for days after landfall and can hit places hundreds of miles from the coast, so keep watching flood alerts even after the wind dies down.

steps.title: Survive the days after the storm
steps.body: Go home only when officials say it is safe. Assume every downed or sagging wire is live and stay far away. Never run a generator, grill, or camp stove indoors, in a garage, or on a porch - use them outside at least 20 feet (6 m) from windows, doors, and vents, and run a battery CO alarm. Carbon monoxide, heat illness with no air conditioning, falls from roofs and ladders, and chainsaw injuries cause many deaths after hurricanes. Work in pairs, take breaks in the shade, and drink water. Have damaged buildings inspected before cleanup, wear boots and gloves, and photograph all damage for insurance and FEMA claims. Text instead of calling to keep networks open.

warnings: Never run a generator, grill, or camp stove inside a home, garage, or on a porch. Keep it at least 20 feet (6 m) from openings and use a battery CO alarm. Carbon monoxide is a leading cause of death after hurricanes.
Do not shelter in a closed attic if water is rising - you can be trapped. Go to the highest floor and onto the roof only if you must.
Mobile homes, RVs, and temporary structures are not safe in hurricane winds. Leave for a sturdy building for any hurricane.
The calm eye is not the end. Stay inside until officials give the all-clear.
Do not trust the forecast cone as a damage map. Surge, rain, and tornadoes often strike well outside it.
proTips: Mark each plywood sheet with the window it fits and pre-drill the anchor holes in calm weather - it turns a day of work into an hour.
Fill bathtubs or a tub water bladder for flushing and washing, and keep drinking water in sealed containers.
Freeze jugs of water before the storm. They keep the fridge cold longer and become drinking water as they melt.
Take a video walk-through of every room and your yard before the storm to support insurance claims.
Be wary of door-to-door contractors after a storm. Check licenses and never pay the full price up front.
source: FEMA Ready.gov / NOAA National Hurricane Center / NWS

sources.title: Winter Storms Aren't Over: CPSC Warns of Deadly Carbon Monoxide Risks

whenNotTo: Do not shelter in place in a storm surge evacuation zone or a mobile home when officials order you to leave.
Do not start evacuating once tropical-storm-force winds have arrived unless your shelter is failing or flooding - being on the road then is often more dangerous. Call 911 for help.

quickGlance.situation: A hurricane or tropical storm is forecast to hit your area in the next few days.
immediate: Check your evacuation zone and surge risk; leave right away if ordered or if you live in a mobile home
Fuel the car, get cash, refill medicines, charge batteries, and secure the yard
Pick your shelter spot: interior windowless room on the lowest floor that will not flood
then: Stay inside through the eye and never drive or walk into floodwater
After the storm, run generators outside 20+ feet (6 m) from the house and avoid downed lines

title: Tornado - Recognition and Response
summary: Know where you will shelter before a tornado threatens, move the moment a warning is issued, and protect your head from flying debris wherever you are.

steps.title: Know the alerts and get more than one way to hear them
steps.body: A Tornado Watch means conditions are right for tornadoes in and near the watch area - stay alert and be ready to move. A Tornado Warning means a tornado has been seen or shown by radar and is in or heading for the warned area - go to shelter now. Do not wait to see or hear it: rain can hide a tornado, and many hit at night. Have at least two ways to get warnings: Wireless Emergency Alerts on your phone, a NOAA Weather Radio with SAME county coding and battery backup, local TV or radio, and local alert sign-ups. Outdoor sirens are meant for people outside and often cannot be heard indoors or while asleep, so never count on them alone.

steps.title: Pick and practice your shelter now
steps.body: The best choice is a FEMA-criteria safe room or an ICC 500 storm shelter, above or below ground. Next best is a basement. With no basement, use a small interior windowless room on the lowest floor - a closet, bathroom, or interior hallway - with as many walls as possible between you and the outside. In a basement, get under a sturdy workbench, heavy table, or the stairs, away from windows and from spots under heavy items like pianos or refrigerators on the floor above. Stock the spot with shoes, helmets, a flashlight, a whistle, water, and medicines. Practice getting everyone there, including pets, in under 2 minutes. Learn the danger signs: a rotating funnel, an approaching debris cloud, or a loud roar like a freight train.

steps.title: In a house or building: get low and cover your head
steps.body: When the warning sounds, go straight to your shelter. Close interior doors behind you. Stay away from windows, doors, and outside walls. Do not waste time opening windows - it does not protect the house and puts you near flying glass. Get under something sturdy if you can. Crouch low, face down, and cover your head and neck with your arms. Pull a mattress, sleeping bags, heavy coats, or blankets over you. Wear a bike, sports, or motorcycle helmet if you have one - head injuries cause many tornado deaths. Put sturdy shoes on everyone so they can walk over broken glass and nails afterward. In a large building such as a store or school, go to the marked shelter area or an interior hallway on the lowest floor, away from wide-span roofs like gyms.

steps.title: In a mobile home: leave before the storm
steps.body: Mobile and manufactured homes, even tied down, offer little protection from tornadoes. On a day when a Tornado Watch is issued or severe storms are forecast, go to a sturdy building or community shelter before storms arrive - not after the warning, when there may be no time. Ask your park manager whether there is a storm shelter on site and how you get in at night. If a tornado is coming and there is no sturdy building close by, get out and lie flat in the nearest ditch, low spot, or culvert and cover your head with your hands. Do not hide in the mobile home or under it.

steps.title: In a vehicle or outdoors: choose the least-bad option
steps.body: No place in a car is truly safe, but some choices are better. If the tornado is visible, far away, and traffic is light, you may be able to drive out of its path at right angles to its motion. If flying debris or strong winds reach you, pull off out of traffic lanes. Then either stay buckled in, put your head below the windows, and cover it with your arms, a coat, or a blanket - or, if you can get clearly lower than the road, leave the car and lie flat in that low area covering your head. Never shelter under a highway overpass or bridge. Wind can be stronger there, debris blows through, and stopped cars block traffic and rescue.

steps.title: After the tornado: get out safely and help carefully
steps.body: Stay sheltered until the warning expires or you are sure the storm has passed - more tornadoes may follow. Check everyone for injuries and give first aid. Put on shoes, long pants, and work gloves before moving through debris. Stay far from downed power lines and treat them as live. If you smell gas, leave the building, do not use switches or flames, and call the gas company or 911 from outside. Do not go into badly damaged buildings. Use texts or social media instead of calls so emergency lines stay open. Take photos of damage before cleanup. Wear a mask when working with mold or dusty debris, and keep children away from the cleanup area.

warnings: Never shelter under a highway overpass or bridge. It gives little protection from debris and can make winds stronger.
Do not wait to see the tornado. Move to shelter as soon as a warning is issued for your area.
Mobile homes are not safe in tornadoes, even when tied down. Leave for a sturdy building before storms arrive.
Outdoor sirens are not designed to be heard indoors. Use a weather radio and phone alerts.
proTips: Keep a cheap bike helmet and a pair of sturdy shoes for each person in your shelter spot. Kids can practice putting them on as a game.
Program a NOAA Weather Radio with your county's SAME code so it only wakes you for alerts that matter to you.
The old advice to hide in the southwest corner of a basement is outdated. What matters is being low, under something sturdy, and away from windows.
Southeast U.S. tornadoes often strike at night and in winter. Keep alerts on loud overnight on storm days.
whenNotTo: Do not try to outrun a tornado by car in city traffic or when you cannot see where it is going.
Do not go outside to look at the storm or take video during a warning.

quickGlance.situation: A Tornado Warning is issued for your location, or you see or hear a tornado coming.
immediate: Go now to a safe room, basement, or interior windowless room on the lowest floor
Get under something sturdy, crouch low, and cover your head and neck
Pull blankets or a mattress over you and wear a helmet and shoes if you have them
then: In a mobile home or car, get to a sturdy building or lie flat in a ditch - never under an overpass
Stay sheltered until the warning ends, then avoid downed lines and gas leaks

title: Earthquake - During and After
summary: Protect yourself in the first seconds of shaking with Drop, Cover, and Hold On, then handle aftershocks, damage, gas, and the days without services that follow a big quake.

steps.title: Prepare your home before the shaking
steps.body: Most earthquake injuries come from things falling or flying, not from buildings collapsing. Strap tall furniture, bookcases, and water heaters to wall studs. Secure TVs and hanging objects, and move heavy or breakable items to low shelves. Keep a flashlight, sturdy shoes, and work gloves by each bed, since broken glass is common. Store at least several days of water and food, medicines, a whistle, a fire extinguisher, and spare batteries. Learn where your gas meter is and keep the right wrench next to it, but only shut it off if you smell gas. Standard homeowner's policies do not cover quake damage - consider earthquake insurance. Older buildings with weak points may need a retrofit. If you live on the West Coast, turn on phone earthquake alerts where available.

steps.title: When shaking starts: Drop, Cover, Hold On
steps.body: DROP right where you are onto your hands and knees so the shaking cannot knock you down. COVER your head and neck with one arm and hand. If a sturdy table or desk is close, crawl under it. If not, get down next to an interior wall or low furniture away from windows, and cover your head and neck with both arms. Crawl only as far as needed to reach better cover. HOLD ON to your shelter (or your head and neck) until the shaking stops, and be ready to move with the table if it shifts. Practice this with your household, for example during the yearly Great ShakeOut drill, so it becomes automatic.

steps.title: Adjust for where you are
steps.body: In bed: stay there, lie face down, and cover your head and neck with a pillow. In a wheelchair or walker: Lock, Cover, and Hold On - lock the wheels, bend forward, and cover your head and neck with your arms, a book, or a pillow. If you cannot get down to the floor, stay seated so you are not knocked over. Outdoors: stay outside, move away from buildings, trees, poles, and power lines, and get low. In a car: pull over in a clear spot away from buildings, trees, overpasses, and wires, set the parking brake, and stay inside. In a high-rise: expect alarms and sprinklers to go off and do not use the elevators. Near slopes or cliffs: watch for falling rocks and landslides.

steps.title: Do not run, and skip the doorway
steps.body: Do not run outside or to another room while the ground is shaking. You are far more likely to be hurt by falling while moving or by glass and building parts falling outside the walls. Do not stand in a doorway. That old advice came from adobe houses; in modern homes a doorway is no stronger than any other part of the house, and the door can swing and hit you. You are safer under a sturdy table. Do not try to use elevators or stairs until the shaking ends.

steps.title: Right after the shaking stops
steps.body: Expect aftershocks - some can be strong enough to cause more damage. Drop, Cover, and Hold On again each time. Check yourself for injuries first, then help others if you can. Put on shoes and gloves. If the building looks badly damaged, get out carefully and move well away; do not go back in. If you smell gas or hear hissing, leave, do not use light switches, phones, or flames inside, and shut off gas at the meter only if you know how. Once off, only the gas company should turn it back on. If you are trapped, cover your mouth with cloth, and signal by texting, tapping on a pipe or wall, or blowing a whistle instead of shouting, which wastes energy and pulls in dust.

steps.title: On the coast: head for high ground right away
steps.body: If you are near the ocean and feel strong or long shaking (making it hard to stand, or lasting 20 seconds or more), treat it as your tsunami warning. As soon as the shaking stops, walk quickly to high ground or inland. Do not wait for an official alert, and do not go to the beach to look. Follow tsunami evacuation route signs. Stay on high ground until officials say it is safe, because a tsunami is a series of waves that can keep coming for hours.

steps.title: Plan for days without services
steps.body: After a major quake, power, water, gas, phone, and roads may be out for days to weeks, and emergency crews will be stretched thin. Save phone calls for emergencies and use texts to check in with your out-of-area contact. Listen to a battery or hand-crank radio for instructions. Use stored water first, and treat any other water before drinking. During cleanup wear long sleeves, long pants, gloves, and thick-soled shoes, and do not try to move heavy debris alone. Take photos of damage for insurance and aid claims. Keep your kit restocked, since aftershocks can go on for weeks.

warnings: Do not run outside or between rooms during shaking. Falling and flying objects cause most injuries.
Do not stand in a doorway - it does not protect you in a modern home.
If you smell gas, do not use switches, phones, or flames indoors. Get outside first.
Do not re-enter a badly damaged building. Aftershocks can bring down weakened walls and ceilings.
On the coast, strong shaking is a natural tsunami warning. Move to high ground as soon as it stops.
proTips: Store a pair of shoes and a flashlight in a bag tied to each bed leg so they cannot slide away.
Practice Drop, Cover, Hold On in every room so everyone knows their nearest sturdy table.
Childproof cabinet latches double as earthquake latches to keep dishes and chemicals from spilling.
Know the water heater holds 30-80 gallons of usable emergency water if it was strapped and stayed upright.
whenNotTo: If the building is actively collapsing around you or on fire, getting out can be the right call - but in most homes and offices, staying put and covering is safer.
Do not shut off the gas just because there was a quake. Only shut it off if you smell gas, hear hissing, or see a damaged line.

quickGlance.situation: The ground is shaking, or a strong quake just ended.
immediate: DROP to hands and knees
COVER head and neck - under a sturdy table if one is close
HOLD ON until the shaking stops; in a wheelchair, lock the wheels and cover
then: Expect aftershocks; put on shoes and check for injuries, gas, and damage
On the coast, walk to high ground right away without waiting for an alert

title: Flood - Flash Flood and Long-Duration Flood
summary: Recognize flash flood danger, get to high ground fast, never drive or walk into floodwater, and stay safe through cleanup after the water goes down.

steps.title: Know your flood risk ahead of time
steps.body: Floods can happen almost anywhere, including places that have never flooded. Look up your address on the FEMA Flood Map Service Center, and learn if you live below a dam or levee or near a creek, dry wash, or low road. Standard homeowner's and renter's policies do not cover flood damage. An NFIP flood policy usually takes 30 days to start, so buy it well before storm season. Move valuables and papers to upper floors or into waterproof containers. Clear gutters and drains, and consider backflow check valves and a battery backup sump pump. Write a plan with at least two routes to higher ground that do not use low crossings.

steps.title: Understand the alerts and the warning signs
steps.body: A Flood or Flash Flood Watch means flooding is possible - get ready to move. A Flash Flood Warning means flash flooding is happening or about to - move to higher ground now. A Flash Flood Emergency is the most serious level, used when lives are in danger. Flash floods can arrive in minutes, sometimes from heavy rain miles upstream while it is dry where you are. Signs include water rising fast, a roaring sound from upstream, water turning muddy, and floating debris. Canyons, dry creek beds, and areas below recent wildfire burn scars can flood with very little rain. Keep a NOAA Weather Radio and phone alerts on when heavy rain is forecast, especially at night.

steps.title: Get to high ground right away
steps.body: When told to evacuate, or when you see water rising, leave immediately. Do not stop to save belongings. Climb to higher ground away from creeks, rivers, and low spots. Depending on the type of flood, officials may tell you to evacuate or to move to a higher floor - follow their direction. Stay off bridges over fast water, which can wash out without warning. Turn off electricity at the main breaker only if you can reach it without standing in water. If you are camping or hiking near streams and hear a roar or see water rising, climb uphill at once rather than running along the channel.

steps.title: Turn Around, Don't Drown
steps.body: More than half of U.S. flood deaths happen in vehicles, usually when someone drives onto a flooded road. Six inches (15 cm) of fast-moving water can knock an adult off their feet. About 12 inches (30 cm) of water can float a small car, and 18-24 inches (45-60 cm) of flowing water can carry away most vehicles, including large SUVs and pickups. You cannot tell how deep the water is or whether the road under it has washed away, especially at night. Never drive around barricades. If you come to water over the road, turn around and find another way, even if other drivers are going through.

steps.title: If your car or building is caught by water
steps.body: If your car is in rapidly moving water, stay inside with your seatbelt on and call 911 - getting out into the current is usually more dangerous. If water starts rising inside the car, get out through a window and onto the roof, and call or signal for help. If you are in still or slowly rising water and can reach dry ground safely, get out and go. In a building, go to the highest level. Do not climb into a closed attic, where rising water can trap you. Go onto the roof only if you must, and wave something bright or use a flashlight to signal rescuers.

steps.title: If you end up in moving water
steps.body: Do not try to stand or swim straight against the current. Float on your back with your feet pointed downstream and your head up, so your feet take the hits from rocks and debris. Steer with your arms toward the shore at an angle. Grab anything that floats. Watch for strainers - fallen trees and fences where water flows through but a person gets pinned - and steer around them. Once out, get away from the edge, since banks can collapse. Do not wade back in to rescue someone; throw them a rope, cooler, or anything that floats and call 911.

steps.title: After the water drops: return and clean up safely
steps.body: Go home only when officials say it is safe, and avoid driving unless needed, since roads may be weakened. Floodwater can carry sewage, chemicals, and debris, and can be electrified by downed lines. Do not touch wet electrical equipment, and have an electrician check wiring before turning power back on. Run generators and gas tools only outdoors and away from windows. Wear boots, heavy gloves, and an N95 or better mask for mold. Throw out food that touched floodwater, and porous items that stayed wet more than 48 hours. Use water only after officials say it is safe, or boil it if told to. People with asthma or weak immune systems, and children, should stay out of moldy buildings and cleanup.

warnings: Never drive or walk into floodwater, and never drive around barricades. About 1 foot (30 cm) of moving water can carry off a car.
Do not go into a closed attic to escape rising water - you can be trapped.
Floodwater may be electrified. Stay away from downed lines and never touch wet electrical equipment.
Watch for snakes, fire ants, and other animals in homes and debris after floods.
Propane tanks and fuel drums can float loose and leak. Stay clear and report them.
proTips: Scout your evacuation routes during a dry day and note every low spot that could be underwater.
Photograph your home and belongings before flood season for faster insurance claims.
Keep a window punch and seatbelt cutter within reach of the driver's seat.
If you have a private well that flooded, do not drink from it until it has been disinfected and tested.
whenNotTo: Do not leave a building and walk through floodwater to evacuate if officials tell you to shelter on an upper floor instead.
Do not leave your car into fast-moving water. Stay buckled and call 911 unless water is rising inside.

quickGlance.situation: A flash flood warning is issued, or water is rising fast around you.
immediate: Move to higher ground now - do not stop for belongings
Turn Around, Don't Drown: never drive or walk into floodwater
In a building, go to the highest floor - not a closed attic
then: If your car is in fast water, stay buckled and call 911; climb on the roof if water rises inside
After the flood, avoid floodwater and wet electrical gear, and wait for the all-clear

title: EMP and Solar Storms - Realistic Effects, Myths, and Response
summary: What a nuclear electromagnetic pulse or extreme solar storm can really do, which popular claims are myths, and how to respond and protect a few key electronics without overspending.

steps.title: Know the two real threats
steps.body: CISA groups this hazard into two kinds. An electromagnetic pulse (EMP) is man-made. The one that worries planners most is a high-altitude nuclear burst (HEMP), set off tens of miles above the ground so the pulse covers a huge area. Smaller non-nuclear devices exist, but they reach roughly a mile or less. A geomagnetic disturbance (GMD) is natural. It happens when a large solar eruption (a coronal mass ejection) hits Earth's magnetic field. In 1989 a solar storm knocked out much of Quebec's grid for about nine hours. CISA calls both 'low probability, high consequence' events. Prepare for them the way you prepare for any long power outage, not as a certain doomsday.

steps.title: Understand E1, E2, and E3
steps.body: A nuclear EMP arrives in three parts. E1 is a very fast spike lasting under a microsecond, like a huge static shock. It hits electronics, control systems, and anything with cables that act as antennas, within line of sight of the burst. E2 is similar to lightning; lightning protection may handle it, but only if E1 did not already damage that protection. E3 is a slow surge lasting seconds to minutes. It mostly stresses long power and phone lines and the large transformers attached to them. A solar storm is like E3 only: it threatens the grid and long lines, not your phone, flashlight, or car.

steps.title: Separate fact from myth
steps.body: Myth: an EMP kills people or stops pacemakers everywhere. A HEMP pulse is too brief to push current through the body; federal analysts describe it as harmless to people directly, though some medical devices could be affected. Myth: every car stops. In EMP Commission tests on 37 cars (model years 1986-2002), most showed only nuisance effects like flickering dash lights; three stalled at high field levels and could be restarted, and one needed repair. Trucks and newer vehicles may differ, and stalled traffic is still a hazard. Myth: all electronics are fried. Small devices that are unplugged and not attached to long wires are much more likely to survive. Fact: the grid is the weak point. Large transformers can take many months to replace, so outages could be long and regional.

steps.title: Recognize a possible event
steps.body: Signs of a HEMP include power, phones, and many electronics failing at once over a wide area, with no storm, and possibly cars stalling on the road. A solar storm is usually forecast: NOAA's Space Weather Prediction Center issues watches and warnings a day or more ahead, and you may see strong auroras farther south than usual. In either case, first check whether the outage is just your home or the whole area. Look at neighbors' lights and try a battery radio. If many devices died at the same moment, assume a long outage and act early, while stores and fuel stations may still be usable.

steps.title: Respond in the first 72 hours
steps.body: Treat it as a grid-down emergency. Fill containers with tap water right away, since pumps may stop when backup power runs out. Keep fridge and freezer doors shut. Check on neighbors who rely on powered medical equipment. Run generators only outdoors, at least 20 feet (6 m) from windows and doors. Unplug sensitive electronics so they are not hit by surges when power returns. If your car still runs, top off fuel early, but avoid unnecessary trips; traffic signals may be out. Listen to a battery or hand-crank radio for official news. Expect cell and internet service to fail as backup batteries at towers run out, even if your phone works.

steps.title: Protect a few spares in a Faraday container
steps.body: CISA's basic advice is to wrap spare electronics in aluminum foil or store them in a Faraday container, and to unplug power, data, and antenna cables from spare gear. A practical setup: wrap a small radio, a power bank, a spare phone, and a small solar charger in two or three layers of heavy foil or anti-static bags, then put them in a metal box or can whose lid touches the body all the way around. Line the inside with cardboard so items never touch the metal. A tight fit and no gaps matter more than brand names. Keep them stored this way all the time; you will not get warning for a nuclear pulse.

steps.title: Plan for a long recovery
steps.body: Because damaged transformers may take months to replace, think in weeks, not days. Your basics are the same as any extended outage: 2+ weeks of water and food, a way to cook safely, medications, sanitation, cash, and a way to receive news. Build relationships with neighbors now; shared skills and supplies go further than solo stockpiles. Keep paper copies of maps, contacts, and important documents. Know how to run your home without electricity, including manual garage door release and well or sump pump options.

warnings: Do not buy 'EMP-proof' gadgets, stickers, or plug-in 'EMP shields' based on marketing claims. Testing of consumer products is limited; a sealed metal container and unplugged gear are the proven basics.
A Faraday container only helps if it is closed when the pulse hits. Gear you use daily and keep plugged in should be assumed vulnerable.
Never run a generator, grill, or camp stove indoors or in a garage during the outage. Carbon monoxide kills more people in long outages than the event itself.
Stalled vehicles and dead traffic signals can cause crashes. Treat every intersection as a four-way stop.
proTips: Sign up for NOAA Space Weather Prediction Center alerts; a solar storm watch gives you time to fill water, charge batteries, and unplug electronics.
A rough check of a Faraday box: put a phone inside and call it. If it rings, the box leaks. A call that does not ring does not prove full protection, but it catches obvious gaps.
A cheap AM/FM/weather radio and spare batteries in the box is the single most useful item to protect.
Keep a printed copy of this guide and your family plan; your phone may work but its apps and maps may not.
source: CISA / Congressional Research Service / EMP Commission / NOAA
