whenNotTo: Do not assume an EMP just because your own house lost power - check the neighborhood and a battery radio first; most outages are ordinary.
Do not leave a safe shelter to 'check on' electronics if a nuclear detonation may also have occurred nearby - follow the nuclear guide (dis-006) first.

quickGlance.situation: Power, phones, and many electronics failed at once over a wide area, or a severe solar storm warning was issued.
immediate: Check if the outage is area-wide: neighbors' lights, battery radio
Fill containers with tap water while pressure lasts
Unplug sensitive electronics; keep fridge and freezer closed
Run any generator outdoors only, 20+ feet from openings
then: Retrieve radio and power bank from your Faraday container
Plan for weeks without grid power and coordinate with neighbors

title: Nuclear Detonation - Get Inside, Stay Inside, Stay Tuned
summary: The current federal 'Get Inside, Stay Inside, Stay Tuned' steps for surviving the flash, blast, and fallout of a nuclear detonation, plus the facts about potassium iodide (KI).

steps.title: If you see a flash, drop and cover
steps.body: A nuclear blast releases a burst of light and heat, then pressure waves. If you see a brilliant flash, look away and close your eyes; staring at it can injure your eyes. Drop face down, ideally behind something solid, and cover your head and neck with your arms. Stay flat until the heat and both shock waves have passed. The shock wave can take many seconds to arrive if you are miles away, so do not get up as soon as the light fades. Flying glass is a major injury source, so stay away from windows if you are indoors.

steps.title: Get inside the best building nearby - now
steps.body: Fallout is radioactive dust and ash that falls from the cloud and can begin coming down within minutes downwind. Get inside right away; do not try to outrun it in a car, which gives little protection. Brick or concrete buildings are best. Go to the basement, or to the middle of the building as far from outside walls and the roof as you can get. In a tall building, a middle floor near the center is good; avoid the top floor. If you cannot get inside at once, cover your mouth and nose with a mask, cloth, or towel while you move to shelter.

steps.title: Remove your outer layer and wash
steps.body: If you were outside, take off your outer layer of clothing before you go deeper into the building, if you can. CDC says this can remove up to 90% of radioactive material on you. Put the clothes in a plastic bag, tie it, and set it away from people. Wash exposed skin and hair with soap and water, or wipe with a damp cloth if there is no shower; do not scrub hard or scratch the skin. Put on clean clothes. Bring pets in and wash them with soap or shampoo and water, then wash your own hands and face. Wipe off sealed food containers and supplies from outside.

steps.title: Stay inside at least 24 hours
steps.body: Radiation from fallout drops quickly over the first hours and days, so time is your friend. CDC advises staying inside for at least 24 hours unless officials tell you otherwise. Close and lock windows and doors. Turn off fans, air conditioners, and forced-air heat that pull in outside air, and close fireplace dampers. Do not go out to pick up children or other family members; schools and hospitals have their own plans, and going out could expose you both. If officials say your building is not safe or tell you to move, follow their route and timing exactly.

steps.title: Stay tuned with a battery radio
steps.body: Officials will measure where fallout landed and announce when and where it is safe to go. Use a battery or hand-crank radio, a phone if networks work, or wireless emergency alerts. A nuclear detonation may also cause an electromagnetic pulse that knocks out some electronics and power, so keep a radio stored in a metal container and carry spare batteries. Text instead of calling to keep networks open. Write down instructions you hear, including evacuation routes, shelter locations, and any advice about potassium iodide.

steps.title: Know the facts about potassium iodide (KI)
steps.body: KI only protects the thyroid gland from radioactive iodine. It does not protect any other part of the body and does nothing against other radioactive materials. FDA says to take it only when public health or emergency officials tell you to. One dose protects for about 24 hours, and taking more than directed adds no protection and can cause serious harm. Infants, children, and pregnant or nursing people benefit most. Adults over 40 should take it only if officials predict a very high thyroid dose. Follow the package label for the dose. Do not take iodine antiseptic or iodized salt as a substitute.

steps.title: Food, water, and when you can leave
steps.body: Food and drinks in sealed cans, bottles, or packages, and food that was inside a closed fridge or cupboard, are generally safe; wipe the outside of containers before opening. Drink bottled water or sealed drinks first; CDC says bottled water is the only water known to be free of contamination until officials say other sources are safe. Water already stored in your toilet tank (not the bowl) or water heater is protected. Use tap water for washing, not drinking, until officials say it is safe - boiling does not remove radioactive material. Do not eat garden produce or drink from open outdoor sources until officials clear them. Leave only when officials say it is safe, or if your shelter becomes unsafe from fire or collapse. When you go out, cover your nose and mouth and follow the routes given.

warnings: Leaving shelter early is the most common deadly mistake. Fallout is most dangerous in the first hours; stay put at least 24 hours unless officials tell you otherwise.

Do not take KI unless officials tell you to. It protects only the thyroid, can cause serious side effects, and should not be taken by people with certain thyroid, skin, or heart conditions - check the label.
Never use tincture of iodine, iodine antiseptic, or iodized salt as a KI substitute. They do not work and can poison you.
A vehicle is poor shelter. If you are driving, get into the nearest solid building.
proTips: Older guidance told people to tape plastic over windows for fallout. CDC's current steps focus on closing windows and doors and shutting off outside air; plastic and tape are mainly a chemical-release tactic.
Pre-plan the best shelter spot at home, work, and school: basement or the center of a large brick or concrete building.
If you choose to keep KI at home, store it with your kit and note the expiration date. Many states give it free to people living near nuclear power plants.
Keep a sealed bag of clean clothes and wet wipes in your kit for decontamination.

sources.title: Frequently Asked Questions about Radiation Emergencies
Frequently Asked Questions on Potassium Iodide (KI)

whenNotTo: Do not shelter in a building that is on fire, badly damaged, or at risk of collapse - move to the next best solid building.
Do not stay put if officials order your area to evacuate - follow their route and timing.

quickGlance.situation: A nuclear detonation has happened in your region and fallout may be coming.
immediate: Flash: look away, drop face down, cover head and neck until shock waves pass
Get inside a brick or concrete building now - basement or center
Remove outer clothing, bag it, wash exposed skin and hair
Close windows and doors; turn off fans and outside air
then: Stay inside at least 24 hours unless officials say otherwise
Listen to a battery radio; take KI only if officials say to

title: Wildfire - Ready, Set, Go and Smoke Safety
summary: Harden your home against embers, leave early when fire threatens, and protect your lungs from wildfire smoke even when the flames are far away.

steps.title: Ready: harden the home ignition zone
steps.body: Most homes lost to wildfire are lit by flying embers, not a wall of flame. Start closest to the house. In the first 5 feet (1.5 m) - the immediate or noncombustible zone - remove anything embers can light: wood mulch, dry leaves, firewood, doormats, and woody shrubs. Use gravel, rock, or concrete instead, and pay extra attention to corners and the area under decks. Clean roofs and gutters, and use metal gutters if you can. Cover vents with 1/8-inch metal mesh. Then keep working outward to 100 feet (30 m) or your property line: mow grass, space and trim trees and shrubs, and remove dead plants. Your local fire department or state forestry agency may offer free home assessments.

steps.title: Ready: plan and pack before fire season
steps.body: Learn your evacuation zone and sign up for your county's emergency alerts - many areas now name zones you will hear in alerts. Plan at least two ways out of your neighborhood, and agree on a meeting place outside the area. Pack a go-bag for each person and pet: water, food, medicines, copies of documents, chargers, a flashlight, N95 respirators, eyeglasses, and a change of cotton or wool clothing. Keep it near the door or in the car. Arrange early help for anyone who cannot drive, and plan for livestock, which need much more time to move. Practice leaving in 10 minutes.

steps.title: Set: stay aware when fire is nearby
steps.body: On red flag days (hot, dry, windy) or when a fire starts near you, keep phone alerts and local news on. Park the car facing out with a full tank and the go-bag inside. Close all windows, vents, and doors to keep embers out, but leave doors unlocked for firefighters. Move patio furniture, cushions, and doormats inside or away from the house. Shut off propane at the tank if told to. Turn on outside lights so crews can find the house in smoke. Connect garden hoses, but do not leave sprinklers running - it drains the water pressure firefighters need.

steps.title: Go: leave early
steps.body: Leave as soon as you are told to - or sooner if you feel unsafe. Early departure keeps you off roads that may soon be choked with smoke, fire, and traffic, and it frees crews to fight the fire instead of rescuing people. Do not wait to see flames. Wear long sleeves, long pants, and boots made of natural fibers. Drive with headlights on, windows closed, and the air set to recirculate. Follow official routes and watch for fire crews and fallen trees. If you are under a wildfire warning, get to safety right away.

steps.title: If you are trapped by fire
steps.body: Call 911 and give your exact location. In a car: park in an area clear of plants, keep the engine running, windows and vents closed, and get down below the windows under a wool blanket or coat. In a home: stay inside, away from outside walls, with doors and windows closed. A sturdy house will usually protect you as the fire front passes, which often takes minutes. On foot: go to an area with little fuel, such as a road, rock field, or already-burned ground, lie face down, and cover yourself. Do not try to outrun a fire uphill - fire moves fastest uphill.

steps.title: Protect your lungs from smoke
steps.body: Smoke can hurt you hundreds of miles from the fire. Check the Air Quality Index on AirNow or the free AirNow app and limit outdoor activity when it is high. Cloth and paper dust masks do not block smoke - a well-fitted NIOSH-approved N95 does. Set up a clean room: pick one room, close windows and doors, and run a portable air cleaner sized for that room on high. Do not use ozone-producing air cleaners. With central air, use a MERV 13 filter, set the fan to On, and use recirculate. A box fan with a MERV 13 furnace filter taped on can work as a DIY cleaner, but do not leave it unattended. Do not fry food, burn candles, or vacuum without a HEPA filter during smoke events.

steps.title: Return home and clean up ash safely
steps.body: Go back only when officials say it is safe. Watch for hot spots, burning stumps, ash pits, damaged power lines, and weakened trees. Burned slopes can produce flash floods and debris flows in heavy rain for years. Children, older adults, and people with heart or lung disease should not do ash cleanup. Others should wear an N95, gloves, long sleeves, and long pants. Lightly mist ash with water before sweeping, never dry-sweep, and wet-mop afterward. Use a HEPA vacuum if you vacuum. Change clothes and shoes before getting in the car. Throw out food exposed to heat or smoke, and follow your water utility's advice before drinking tap water.

warnings: Do not wait for flames to leave. Many wildfire deaths happen to people who left too late and got trapped on the road.
Cloth masks and bandanas do not protect against smoke. Use a fitted N95.
Never use ozone generators sold as air purifiers - ozone harms the lungs.
After a fire, burn scars can cause flash floods and debris flows with only short bursts of rain.
Do not drive through smoke so thick you cannot see the road edge - pull into a clear area instead.
proTips: Keep a laminated card of your evacuation zone name and two routes in the car glovebox.
Buy N95s and spare MERV 13 filters before fire season, when stores still have them.
Take photos of every room and your yard now; it speeds up insurance claims if the house is lost.
Leave a note on the door saying when you left and where you went.
source: FEMA Ready.gov / IAFC Ready, Set, Go! / EPA AirNow / NWS

sources.title: Firewise USA Immediate Noncombustible Zone Fact Sheet
sources.publisher: Texas A&M Forest Service / NFPA Firewise

sources.title: When Smoke Is in the Air

whenNotTo: Do not stay behind to defend your home with hoses. Fire crews are trained and equipped for it; residents are not.
Do not evacuate on foot through unburned brush toward a fire you cannot see - follow official routes.

quickGlance.situation: A wildfire is burning near you, or smoke is filling the air.
immediate: Leave as soon as officials say go - or sooner if you feel unsafe
Close windows and vents, grab go-bags, and drive out with lights on and air on recirculate
Wear a fitted N95 in smoke - not a cloth mask
then: Set up a clean room with an air cleaner if smoke reaches you
Return only on the all-clear and clean ash wet, never dry-swept

title: Winter Storms and Ice Storms
summary: Get through snow, ice, and extreme cold - including days without power - by preparing early, heating safely, avoiding carbon monoxide, and knowing what to do if you are stranded in a car.

steps.title: Learn the alerts
steps.body: A Winter Storm Watch means a significant storm is possible, often 2 days out - start getting ready. A Winter Weather Advisory means snow, sleet, or ice will cause trouble but not severe danger. A Winter Storm Warning means heavy snow, sleet, or freezing rain is expected - stay off the roads if you can. An Ice Storm Warning means about 1/4 inch (6 mm) or more of ice is expected, enough to snap trees and power lines. A Blizzard Warning means strong winds of 35 mph (56 km/h) or more with visibility under 1/4 mile (400 m) for hours. Extreme Cold Watches and Warnings cover dangerous cold and wind chill. Criteria vary by region, so learn your local office's thresholds.

steps.title: Prepare the house before the storm
steps.body: Stock at least several days of water, food that needs no cooking, medicines, flashlights, batteries, and a battery or hand-crank radio. Have extra blankets, sleeping bags, hats, and warm layers for everyone. Install battery-powered or battery-backup carbon monoxide alarms on every level and outside sleeping areas, and test them. Insulate exposed pipes and know where your main water shut-off is. If you heat with wood, have dry firewood and get the chimney checked. Keep ice melt or sand, a shovel, and a full tank of gas in the car. Charge phones and power banks before the storm hits.

steps.title: Stay warm safely when the power goes out
steps.body: Pick one room to heat and live in - ideally interior with few windows. Close off other rooms, stuff towels under doors, and cover windows at night. Wear loose layers, a hat, and dry socks, and remove layers before you sweat. Eat and drink regularly - your body needs fuel to make heat. Keep space heaters at least 3 feet (1 m) from beds, curtains, and furniture, plug them straight into the wall (never a power strip), and never leave them on unattended. Use flashlights instead of candles. If your home becomes too cold to stay safe, go to a warming center or a friend's house before night falls.

steps.title: Prevent carbon monoxide poisoning
steps.body: Carbon monoxide (CO) has no smell or color and kills people every winter storm. Never use a generator, grill, camp stove, or charcoal inside a home, garage, basement, crawlspace, or on a porch - even with the doors open. Run generators outdoors at least 20 feet (6 m) from the house with the exhaust pointed away and nearby windows closed. Never heat your home with a gas oven. Keep snow cleared from furnace, dryer, and water heater vents. If the CO alarm sounds or people feel headache, dizziness, nausea, or confusion, get everyone outside to fresh air right away and call 911.

steps.title: Spot and treat cold injuries
steps.body: Frostbite shows as numbness and white, grayish, or waxy skin on fingers, toes, ears, or the nose. At a wind chill of -20 F (-29 C), it can set in within about 30 minutes. Get to warmth and get medical help. If you must wait, rewarm slowly with body heat or warm (not hot) water, and do not rub the skin or rewarm it if it might freeze again. Hypothermia is a body temperature below 95 F (35 C). Signs are shivering, confusion, memory loss, slurred speech, drowsiness, and exhaustion. Get the person into a warm, dry place, remove wet clothes, warm the center of the body first with blankets and skin-to-skin contact, and get medical care right away. Call 911 if they are confused or not shivering.

steps.title: If you are stranded in a vehicle
steps.body: Stay with the car unless a building is close and you can clearly see it - people get lost in blowing snow. Tie a bright cloth to the antenna or door, and raise the hood once snow stops. Run the engine about 10 minutes each hour for heat, and crack a downwind window. Before running it, clear snow from the tailpipe so exhaust cannot build up inside. Turn on the dome light at night while the engine runs so rescuers can see you. Move your arms, legs, fingers, and toes to keep blood flowing, and huddle together. Keep a winter car kit with blankets, a shovel, sand, water, snacks, a flashlight, and a phone charger.

steps.title: Handle ice, snow, and damage after the storm
steps.body: Ice-coated trees and lines can keep falling for hours after the freezing rain stops - stay out from under them and treat every downed line as live. Walk with short, flat-footed steps on ice and wear boots with good tread. Shoveling heavy snow strains the heart: take breaks, push snow instead of lifting, and let someone else do it if you have heart problems. Check on older neighbors and anyone living alone. If pipes freeze, open the faucet and warm the pipe with a hair dryer or warm towels - never an open flame. If a pipe bursts, shut off the main water valve.

warnings: Never use a generator, grill, or camp stove indoors or in a garage, even with the door open. Carbon monoxide can kill in minutes.
Never heat your home with a gas oven or stovetop.
Clear snow from your car's tailpipe before running the engine while stranded.
Do not rub frostbitten skin or rewarm it if it might refreeze - that causes more damage.
Ice-loaded branches and power lines can fall long after the storm ends. Keep clear.
proTips: Set up a tent or blanket fort inside your warm room - a small space traps body heat well.
Fill a few pots and jugs with water before the storm in case pipes freeze or the well pump loses power.
Keep the fridge and freezer closed. A full freezer stays frozen about 48 hours.
Hand and foot warmers in your car kit are cheap and very effective.

sources.title: Winter Storms Aren't Over: CPSC Warns of Deadly Carbon Monoxide Risks and Fires During Power Outages

whenNotTo: Do not leave a stranded car to walk for help in a blizzard unless shelter is close and clearly visible.
Do not rewarm frostbite in the field if there is any chance it will freeze again before you reach shelter.

quickGlance.situation: A winter or ice storm is coming, or the power is out in freezing weather.
immediate: Gather everyone into one closed-off room and dress in layers
Keep generators and grills outside, 20+ feet (6 m) from the house; test CO alarms
Stay off the roads during the storm
then: Watch for frostbite and hypothermia and get medical help if you see signs
If stranded in a car, stay with it, clear the tailpipe, and run the engine 10 minutes each hour

title: Extreme Heat Waves - Protecting Your Household and Neighbors
summary: Heat kills more Americans than most other weather. Use forecasts to plan, keep your body cool, spot heat illness early, and check on the people around you who are most at risk.

steps.title: Watch the heat forecast and HeatRisk
steps.body: Follow your local NWS office for Heat Advisories and Extreme Heat Watches and Warnings. The NWS HeatRisk tool rates each day from 0 (green, little risk) to 4 (magenta, rare or long-lasting extreme heat). It looks at how unusual the heat is for your area and time of year, how long it lasts, and whether nights stay warm - not just the temperature. The Heat Index tells you how hot it feels with humidity, but what is dangerous differs from place to place and person to person. Several hot days in a row with warm nights are the most dangerous, because the body never gets a chance to recover.

steps.title: Get ready before the heat arrives
steps.body: Find your nearest cooling centers, libraries, malls, or other air-conditioned public spaces and how to get there. Service your air conditioner and clean its filters. Stock water and any medicines you need, and ask your doctor or pharmacist whether any of your medicines raise heat risk or need to be stored cool. Put up light-colored shades or reflective film on sun-facing windows. Make a buddy plan: decide who will check on whom - older relatives, neighbors who live alone, people with chronic illness, pregnant people, and families with babies. Plan outdoor work and exercise for early morning or evening.

steps.title: Keep your body cool
steps.body: Stay in air conditioning as much as you can. If your home has none, spend the hottest hours at a cooling center or another cool place. Fans help move air, but when it is very hot they cannot keep your body cool enough on their own - use them along with cool showers, damp cloths, and air conditioning. Drink water often, even before you are thirsty, and skip alcohol and large sugary drinks. If your doctor limits your fluids, ask how much to drink in hot weather. Wear light, loose, light-colored clothing and a wide-brim hat. Eat lighter meals and avoid using the oven. Close blinds on the sunny side during the day and open windows at night only if it is cooler outside.

steps.title: Never leave anyone in a parked car
steps.body: A closed car heats up fast, even on a mild day and even with a window cracked. More than 1,000 children in the U.S. have died of heat stroke in hot cars over the last 25 years. Never leave a child, an older adult, or a pet in a parked car, even for a minute. Build a habit: put your phone, bag, or a shoe in the back seat so you always check before you lock up. Always lock your car when parked so children cannot climb in to play. If you see a child alone in a hot car, call 911 right away.

steps.title: Spot heat exhaustion and act fast
steps.body: Signs of heat exhaustion include heavy sweating, cool and clammy skin, thirst, dizziness, headache, nausea or vomiting, weakness, and muscle cramps. Move the person to a cooler place, loosen or remove extra clothing, put cool wet cloths on the skin or have them take a cool bath, and give sips of cool water if they are awake and can swallow. Get medical help if they are vomiting, if symptoms get worse, or if they do not improve within an hour. Heat exhaustion can quickly turn into heat stroke.

steps.title: Treat heat stroke as a 911 emergency
steps.body: Heat stroke is life-threatening. Signs include confusion, slurred speech, strange behavior, fainting or unconsciousness, seizures, and very high body temperature. The skin may be hot and red, and the person may or may not be sweating. Call 911 right away. While waiting, move them to a cooler place, remove extra clothing, and cool them as fast as you can: soak them with cool water, cover them with wet towels and fan them, or put ice packs on the neck, armpits, and groin. Cold water immersion up to the neck works best if a tub or tank is available and someone stays with them. Do not give fluids to someone who is confused or not fully awake.

steps.title: Check on neighbors and plan for a power outage
steps.body: Check on people at risk at least twice a day during a heat wave - in person if you can. Ask if they have working air conditioning, water, and medicines, and whether they know their nearest cooling center. Offer a ride. Heat waves strain the grid and can cause outages. If the power goes out, move people to a cooler place early instead of waiting for night. Use generators only outdoors, at least 20 feet (6 m) from windows and doors. Keep pets inside with water and shade, and check that sidewalks are not too hot for their paws.

warnings: Heat stroke can kill or cause lasting disability. Call 911 and start cooling the person right away.
Never leave a child, older adult, or pet in a parked car, even with windows cracked.
Fans alone cannot prevent heat illness in very high heat. Use cooling centers and air conditioning.
Older adults, young children, pregnant people, outdoor workers, and people with chronic illness or on certain medicines are at highest risk.
proTips: A cool foot bath or wet bandana around the neck brings comfort fast when there is no AC.
Freeze water bottles overnight to use as ice packs and drinking water the next day.
Check urine color: pale yellow means you are drinking enough; dark means drink more.
Ask neighbors to share phone numbers in a group text before summer so checking in is easy.

sources.title: Winter Storms Aren't Over: CPSC Warns of Deadly Carbon Monoxide Risks (generator placement)

whenNotTo: Do not wait to see if heat stroke symptoms improve on their own - call 911 first, then cool.
Do not give large amounts of plain water quickly to someone who has been sweating for hours without food; sip steadily and include salty snacks or oral rehydration drinks.

quickGlance.situation: Dangerous heat is forecast or under way, or someone is showing signs of heat illness.
immediate: Get to air conditioning or a cooling center during the hottest hours
Drink water often and skip alcohol
Confusion or fainting in the heat = call 911 and cool the person with water and ice now
then: Check on older neighbors and people living alone twice a day
Never leave anyone in a parked car

title: Drought and Long-Term Water Shortages
summary: Stretch your household water through a long drought or supply cut: know the drought stages, cut use without risking health, protect a private well, and keep a reserve of safe drinking water.

steps.title: Track drought stages and local rules
steps.body: Drought builds slowly, so watch for long dry spells and check the U.S. Drought Monitor and your water supplier's notices. Many communities move through stages. At a watch stage, suppliers ask for voluntary cuts. At a warning stage, they prepare emergency plans and ask for deeper cuts. At an emergency stage, mandatory limits start and other water sources may be brought in. At a disaster stage, water may be rationed and outside aid may arrive. Always follow state and local water-use rules - fines are common, and the limits protect supply for hospitals, firefighting, and drinking water.

steps.title: Keep an emergency drinking water reserve
steps.body: Even in a drought, keep stored drinking water for emergencies: at least 1 gallon (3.8 L) per person per day for several days, and two weeks if you can. Store it in clean, food-grade containers in a cool, dark place, and rotate it on the schedule on the label or every 6 months for tap water you filled yourself. Add extra for pets, hot weather, and anyone nursing or sick. During a water emergency, conserve - but do not ration drinking water to the point of dehydration. Drink what you need today and look for more tomorrow.

steps.title: Cut indoor use first
steps.body: Fix leaks first - a dripping faucet or running toilet can waste many gallons a day. Take short showers and turn off the tap while brushing teeth, shaving, or scrubbing dishes. Catch the cold water that runs while you wait for hot water and use it for plants or cooking. Run the dishwasher and washing machine only with full loads. Use the trash or compost instead of the garbage disposal. Flush less often when safe and sanitary. Over time, switch to low-flow toilets, faucets, and showerheads and water-efficient appliances. Keep a simple daily log of your water meter so you can see what is working.

steps.title: Cut outdoor use the smart way
steps.body: Outdoor watering is often the largest household use. Follow your local watering days. Water in the early morning or evening when less evaporates, and use drip lines or soaker hoses instead of spray sprinklers. Water in several short sessions so the soil soaks it up instead of letting it run off. Mulch beds to hold moisture. Never leave a hose or sprinkler running unattended. Let lawns go dormant if allowed - most grasses recover when rain returns. Choose native and drought-tolerant plants for the future. Skip car washing and decorative fountains during restrictions, and collect rainwater where it is legal.

steps.title: Reuse water safely
steps.body: Lightly used water - such as from rinsing produce or a bucket in the shower while it warms up - can water plants or flush a toilet by pouring it into the bowl. Do not reuse water that has touched raw meat, diapers, or toilet waste. Do not store greywater for more than a day, since germs grow fast in warm water. Do not use greywater on food crops you eat raw. Check state and local rules before setting up any permanent greywater system. Keep reused water clearly labeled and away from children and drinking water containers.

steps.title: Protect a private well and your water quality
steps.body: Drought can lower the water table, so private wells may give less water or go dry. Space out heavy water use, and watch for sputtering taps, air in the lines, or a pump that runs longer than usual - these can be early signs. Low water and warm temperatures can also let germs and chemicals such as nitrate, arsenic, and uranium build up. Test your well at least once a year and after any change in taste, smell, or color. Your local health department can help. If the water may be unsafe, use stored or bottled water for drinking, cooking, and brushing teeth, or boil it if the issue is germs.

steps.title: Watch for the side effects of drought
steps.body: Dry weather brings more dust and wildfire smoke, which can worsen asthma and lung disease - keep N95s and use a portable air cleaner if air quality drops. Drought often comes with heat waves, so plan for cooling. Fire risk climbs, so follow burn bans and clear dry brush around your home. Low lakes and rivers hide rocks and debris, so do not dive into water you have not checked. Long droughts also strain farm and family budgets and stress mental health - check in on neighbors and reach out for help if you or someone you know is struggling.

warnings: Do not cut your drinking water to the point of dehydration. Conserve everything else first.
Do not drink untested well water that has changed in taste, smell, or color during a drought.
Never reuse water that has touched sewage, diapers, or raw meat.
Drought sharply increases wildfire risk. Follow burn bans.
proTips: Put a bucket in the shower and a pan in the sink - you will be surprised how much clean water you catch for plants.
Do a leak test: write down your meter reading, use no water for 2 hours, and check it again.
Rain barrels fill fast when rain finally comes - set them up before the drought ends.
A layer of mulch 2-3 inches (5-8 cm) deep can cut garden watering needs a lot.
source: U.S. EPA / Ready Navy (DoD) drought guidance / Massachusetts DPH

sources.title: Health x Drought
sources.publisher: Massachusetts Executive Office of Energy and Environmental Affairs

whenNotTo: Do not set up permanent greywater plumbing without checking local codes.
Do not drill or deepen a well in a hurry without a licensed driller and the needed permits.

quickGlance.situation: Your area is in drought, or your water supplier has announced restrictions or shortages.
immediate: Check your local drought stage and follow water-use rules
Fix leaks and cut showers, laundry, and lawn watering first
Keep at least several days of drinking water stored - do not ration it to dehydration
then: Reuse clean rinse water on plants and test your private well
Prepare for the dust, smoke, heat, and fire risk that come with drought

title: Tsunami - Natural Warning Signs and Evacuation
summary: Recognize the natural signs of a tsunami, get to high ground or inland without waiting, and stay there until officials say the waves are over.

steps.title: Know if you live, work, or play in a hazard zone
steps.body: Tsunamis threaten the Pacific coast, Alaska, Hawaii, Puerto Rico, the U.S. Virgin Islands, and other U.S. territories most, but any coast can be hit. Look up your state or county tsunami hazard map and find the hazard zone for your home, work, school, and favorite beaches. Many coastal roads have blue-and-white tsunami evacuation route signs with a wave and an arrow pointing to high ground. Walk your route ahead of time, ideally at night too, and time it. Plan to go on foot - roads jam and bridges may be damaged after a quake. When you travel to a coast, ask your hotel about its evacuation route.

steps.title: Learn the natural warning signs
steps.body: Nature may warn you before any official alert. Treat any of these as a signal to leave now: strong or long shaking from an earthquake when you are near the coast - if it is hard to stand or it lasts a long time; a loud roar from the ocean, like a train or jet; the ocean suddenly pulling back and exposing the sea floor, reefs, or fish; or a sudden rise or wall of water. Do not walk out to look at an exposed sea floor - the water will return with force within minutes. A tsunami from a nearby quake can arrive in minutes, before any official warning can reach you.

steps.title: If the ground shakes, protect yourself then move
steps.body: During the shaking, Drop, Cover, and Hold On. As soon as the shaking stops, go - do not wait for sirens, a phone alert, or the news. Grab your go-bag only if it is right next to you. Help others nearby if you can do it without delay. Leave on foot if you can. If you are in a car and the road is clear, keep going inland or uphill, but abandon the car and walk if traffic stops. Every minute counts when the source is close.

steps.title: Go high, go far
steps.body: Head for high ground as far inland as you can. A good goal is at least 100 feet (30 m) above sea level or at least 1 mile (1.6 km) inland, or out of the mapped hazard zone. Follow evacuation route signs. If you cannot reach high ground in time, go to the upper floors or roof of a tall, sturdy concrete building - this is called vertical evacuation and is a last resort. Tsunami waves can be 10 to 100 feet (3 to 30 m) high and move faster than you can run on land, so do not stop to watch.

steps.title: Respond to official alerts
steps.body: The National Tsunami Warning Center and Pacific Tsunami Warning Center issue alerts. A Tsunami Warning means dangerous flooding and strong currents are possible - move out of the hazard zone. A Tsunami Advisory means strong currents and waves are expected near the water - get out of the water and off beaches, harbors, and marinas. A Tsunami Watch means a distant event may affect you - stay tuned and be ready to act. A Tsunami Information Statement usually means no threat. If you are outside the hazard zone when a warning is issued, stay where you are unless officials tell you otherwise, so roads stay open for those who need them.

steps.title: If you are in the water or on a boat
steps.body: If you are caught in the water, grab onto anything that floats, such as a log, door, or cooler, and try to stay with it. Do not try to swim against the flow. If you are on a boat in open, deep water, move farther out to sea, since tsunami waves are much smaller in deep water. If you are in a harbor or at a dock, get off the boat and go inland to high ground - harbors see violent currents and surges.

steps.title: Stay up high until the all-clear
steps.body: A tsunami is a series of waves, and the first is often not the largest. Dangerous waves and currents can keep coming for hours, sometimes many hours after the first wave. Stay on high ground until local officials say it is safe to return. When you do go back, avoid floodwater, which may hide debris and be deeper than it looks. Stay away from downed or underground power lines, damaged buildings, roads, and bridges. Use texts instead of calls. Photograph damage for insurance, and call 911 only for emergencies.

warnings: Never go to the shore to watch a tsunami or explore an exposed sea floor.
Do not wait for an official warning after strong coastal shaking - the shaking is your warning.
The first wave is often not the biggest. Stay on high ground until the all-clear.
Do not drive into traffic jams in the hazard zone. Walk if roads are blocked.
proTips: Keep comfortable walking shoes and a small go-bag where you can grab them in seconds.
Practice your walking route with children so they know where to go if they are at school or the beach.
Learn the location of the nearest high ground at any beach the moment you arrive.
Sign up for your county's coastal alerts and keep phone emergency alerts turned on.
source: FEMA Ready.gov / NOAA Tsunami Warning Centers
whenNotTo: If you are outside the tsunami hazard zone when a warning comes, do not evacuate unless officials tell you to.
Do not use vertical evacuation in a building if you have time to reach natural high ground.

quickGlance.situation: You are near the coast and feel strong shaking, hear an ocean roar, see the sea pull back, or get a Tsunami Warning.
immediate: Go now - on foot - to high ground or inland
Aim for 100 feet (30 m) up or 1 mile (1.6 km) inland, or out of the hazard zone
If you cannot get out, go to the upper floors of a tall, sturdy concrete building
then: Stay up high for hours - more waves are coming
Return only when officials give the all-clear

title: Volcanic Eruptions and Ashfall
summary: Know the hazards of a nearby volcano, evacuate early from lava, lahars, and pyroclastic flows, and protect your lungs, eyes, house, water, and vehicles when ash falls.

steps.title: Know your volcano and its hazards
steps.body: The U.S. has dozens of active volcanoes in Alaska, Hawaii, and the Cascade Range of Washington, Oregon, and California, with others in places like the Yellowstone region and the Northern Mariana Islands. Each has different hazards. Close to the volcano, lava flows, pyroclastic flows (fast avalanches of hot gas and rock), and volcanic gases can kill. Down river valleys, lahars - fast mudflows of ash, rock, and water - can travel tens of miles from the mountain. Far away, ash can fall over huge areas. Check your county hazard maps and the USGS volcano observatory for your area, learn if you live in a lahar zone, and sign up for local alerts.

steps.title: Prepare supplies before an eruption
steps.body: Keep several days of food, water, and medicines. Add ash supplies: NIOSH-approved N95 respirators for every adult, close-fitting goggles, and long-sleeved clothes. Wear eyeglasses instead of contact lenses during ashfall, since ash scratches the eyes. Store plastic sheeting and tape to cover electronics and seal drafty doors. Keep spare air and oil filters for your car and any generator, and extra wiper blades. Have a battery or hand-crank radio, since ash can damage power and phone lines. Plan an evacuation route that avoids river valleys below the volcano.

steps.title: Evacuate early from deadly flows
steps.body: Follow local officials, who will tell you to evacuate or shelter in place. Leave right away if lava, a lahar, or a pyroclastic flow is heading your way, or if officials say an eruption is about to happen. You cannot outrun a pyroclastic flow, so leave well before. If you are near a stream or river below a volcano, watch for rising water, a rumbling sound, or mud in low areas, and move uphill quickly - lahars follow valleys. When driving, keep windows and vents closed, and drive across or away from the path of danger, watching for debris and ash on the road.

steps.title: Shelter indoors during ashfall
steps.body: If you are told to stay, go inside and stay there. Close windows, doors, and fireplace or woodstove dampers. Turn off fans, furnaces, and air conditioners that pull in outside air. Bring pets and livestock into closed shelters. Put damp towels at the bottom of doors. Cover sensitive electronics. Wear an N95 if you must go outside or when cleaning indoor ash; a simple dust mask is only a last resort, and limit time outside. Note that particle masks do not filter volcanic gases. If ashfall goes on for more than a few hours, listen to officials about leaving - heavy ash can block air intakes and collapse roofs.

steps.title: Protect roofs, gutters, and water
steps.body: Ash is heavy, especially when wet, and can collapse roofs. Remove it from flat or low-slope roofs and gutters as soon as it is safe, but be careful: ash makes roofs slippery, so use a harness or have a helper, and never go up during ashfall. Keep ash out of downspouts and storm drains when you can - it clogs pipes like cement. Cover rain barrels, tanks, and wells. If you rely on rainwater, disconnect your downspouts before ash falls. Use stored water if your tap water looks gritty or your supplier issues an advisory.

steps.title: Avoid driving in ash
steps.body: Ashfall can stop travel for days. It cuts visibility, makes roads slick, and wears out engines and brakes. Do not drive unless you must. If you do, go slowly with headlights on, keep windows up, and do not run the air conditioning, which pulls ash in. Use plenty of washer fluid, since dry wipers scratch the glass. If ash is heavy, turn off the engine and wait, because ash can clog it and stall the car. Change the air and oil filters more often after driving in ash.

steps.title: Clean up ash carefully
steps.body: Wear an N95, goggles, gloves, and long clothing during cleanup. Lightly wet the ash before you sweep or shovel to keep dust down, but do not soak it, since wet ash gets much heavier. Shovel it into sturdy bags and follow local rules on where to put it. Use a HEPA vacuum indoors. Clean filters on furnaces and air conditioners before running them again. Coordinate cleanup with neighbors so streets are not cleaned twice. Children and people with asthma, heart, or lung disease should stay indoors and avoid cleanup. Get medical care for eye injuries or breathing problems that do not improve.

warnings: You cannot outrun a pyroclastic flow or lahar. Evacuate early from danger zones and river valleys below the volcano.
Particle masks like N95s do not filter toxic volcanic gases. Move away from areas with gas or fumes.
Ash on roofs is heavy and slippery. Never climb up during ashfall, and use fall protection.
Do not run car or home air conditioning during ashfall - it pulls ash inside.
proTips: Swap contact lenses for glasses as soon as ash is forecast.
Keep a few spare car air filters; they can clog in a single day of driving in ash.
Cover sensitive electronics and computers with plastic sheeting before ash arrives.
Store several days of water before ashfall; it can foul open water sources and tanks.

sources.title: Volcanic Ash: What Can I Do?
Safety Guidelines: During a Volcanic Eruption

whenNotTo: Do not shelter in place in a mapped lahar or pyroclastic flow zone when officials order evacuation.
Do not soak ash with lots of water during cleanup - it becomes much heavier and can clog drains.

quickGlance.situation: A nearby volcano is erupting or ash is falling on your area.
immediate: Evacuate right away if lava, a lahar, or a pyroclastic flow may reach you
Get indoors, close windows and dampers, and turn off fans and HVAC
Wear an N95 and goggles outside; swap contacts for glasses
then: Avoid driving; if you must, go slow, windows up, A/C off
Clear roof ash early and safely, and clean up with damp ash and a HEPA vacuum

title: Landslides and Mudflows (Especially After Wildfires)
summary: Spot the signs of a moving slope, know why burned hillsides are so dangerous in heavy rain, and get out of the path of debris flows before they reach you.

steps.title: Know if you live in a slide or burn-scar zone
steps.body: Landslides happen on steep slopes, at the base of hills, in canyons, and along the mouths of mountain streams. Risk climbs where soil has been cut for roads, where water collects, and especially below land burned by wildfire. A simple rule from the NWS: if you can see a burned area uphill from you, you are at risk. Burned slopes are most likely to produce flash floods and debris flows for at least the first 2 years after the fire, and risk can last longer while plants regrow. Check your county hazard maps, ask local officials about post-fire risk, and sign up for alerts.

steps.title: Watch for slow-moving slide signs around your home
steps.body: Some landslides creep for days or weeks before they fail. Look for doors or windows that start to stick, new cracks in walls, plaster, tile, or the foundation, and gaps where outside stairs or decks pull away from the house. Outdoors, look for new cracks in the ground or pavement, tilting trees, fences, poles, or retaining walls, bulging ground at the bottom of a slope, and water seeping from the ground in new places. Broken water or sewer lines can also be a sign. If you notice these, contact local officials and a geotechnical engineer, and be ready to leave.

steps.title: Know why burn scars are different
steps.body: Fire burns off the plants and roots that slow water and hold soil. The ground can also become water-repellent, so rain runs off fast instead of soaking in. As little as about half an inch (13 mm) of rain in an hour or less can trigger flash flooding below a burn area, and debris flows can start after just a few minutes of intense rain - even on a dry slope. For debris flows, how hard it rains matters more than how much falls in total. Flooding can come almost as fast as radar sees the rain, so warnings may give very little time.

steps.title: Act before the rain, not after
steps.body: When heavy rain is forecast over a burn scar or slide-prone area, follow NWS Flash Flood Watches and Warnings and local alerts. Do not wait for a warning to move - if moderate to heavy rain starts, leave vulnerable areas. Leave right away when told to evacuate, even if you have been told to leave before and nothing happened. Plan a route that stays out of canyons and stream channels. Sandbags and walls can steer water but cannot stop or redirect a debris flow, so staying home to protect property puts your life at risk. Many landslide deaths happen at night while people sleep, so stay awake and alert during storms.

steps.title: Recognize a debris flow coming
steps.body: Listen and look for rushing water or mud, and unusual sounds such as cracking trees, knocking boulders, roaring, or a noise like a freight train. A faint rumble that grows louder means the flow is getting closer. Watch for a sudden rise in creek water, or clear water turning muddy, or a stream that suddenly drops while it is still raining - debris may be damming it upstream. Do not cross flowing water or mud, and do not cross a bridge if a flow is coming.

steps.title: If you are caught, get above it
steps.body: Move uphill and out of the channel as fast as you can - to the side of the flow, not down the valley in front of it. If you cannot get out, go to the highest place you can reach: an upper floor, a roof, or a sturdy tree. Call 911 as soon as you can. If you are swept up and cannot escape, curl into a tight ball and protect your head. Avoid river valleys and low spots.

steps.title: After the slide
steps.body: Stay away from the slide area - more slides may follow, and flooding often comes after landslides. Check for injured or trapped people from a safe distance and direct rescuers to them instead of going into the slide. Report broken utility lines and damaged roads or rail lines to authorities. Have a professional inspect your home, foundation, and the ground around it before going back in. Replant damaged ground soon to cut erosion, and talk to a geotechnical expert before rebuilding. Ask your insurer about coverage, since some debris flow damage may be covered by NFIP flood policies.

warnings: Burn scars can unleash flash floods and debris flows with only short bursts of heavy rain, often with very little warning.
Sandbags cannot stop a debris flow. Leave instead of staying to protect property.
Do not cross moving mud or water, or a bridge with a flow approaching.
Stay out of slide areas after the event - more slides and flooding can follow.
proTips: Mark burn areas uphill from your home on a map and keep it with your go-bag.
Set phone alerts loud at night during rainy seasons if you live below a burn scar.
Take dated photos of cracks around your house so you can see if they are growing.
Keep your car parked facing out and fueled during storm season in canyon areas.
source: NWS / USGS Landslide Hazards Program / Michigan State Police EMHSD (Ready.gov-based)

Landslides and Debris Flow

whenNotTo: Do not try to dig out or stabilize a moving slope yourself - get a professional.
Do not drive through canyon roads below a burn scar during heavy rain.

quickGlance.situation: Heavy rain is falling or forecast on steep or recently burned land above you, or you see signs the ground is moving.
immediate: Leave canyons, stream channels, and areas below burn scars before or as rain starts
Listen for roaring, cracking, or rumbling and watch for muddy or suddenly dropping streams
If caught, move uphill and to the side - out of the channel
then: Stay out of the slide area afterward; more slides and floods can follow
Have a pro inspect your home and land before going back

title: Dam and Levee Failure
summary: Find out whether you live below a dam or behind a levee, know how you would be warned, and move to high ground fast if one fails or is threatened.

steps.title: Find out if a dam or levee protects or threatens you
steps.body: Many homes sit downstream of dams or behind levees without the owners knowing it. Look up your area in the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers National Inventory of Dams and National Levee Database, and ask your county emergency manager whether you are in a dam inundation zone. Dams are rated High, Significant, or Low hazard based on what would happen if they failed, not on their condition. On FEMA flood maps, land shown as protected by a levee may still flood if the levee is overtopped or breaks. Being behind a levee lowers risk; it does not remove it.

steps.title: Get flood insurance and a plan
steps.body: Buy flood insurance even if you are not required to, including in areas mapped as protected by a levee or dam. New NFIP policies usually take 30 days to begin. Ask the dam owner or your emergency manager whether the dam has an Emergency Action Plan and what the warning system is - sirens, phone alerts, or door-to-door notices. Learn your evacuation route to high ground and pick a place to go outside the inundation area. Write a family communication plan with an out-of-area contact. Keep a go-bag ready and important papers in a waterproof container.

steps.title: Know the warning signs and alerts
steps.body: Most dam and levee failures happen during or after heavy rain or floods, but some happen on clear days. Officials may issue a Flash Flood Warning or Flash Flood Emergency for a dam break or a dam at risk. Watch for water flowing over the top of a dam or levee, new leaks, muddy water seeping from the downstream side or the land behind a levee, sinkholes, slumping, or cracks. Report these to 911 or your emergency manager right away. Keep a NOAA Weather Radio and local alerts on during long rain events, and listen for evacuation orders.

steps.title: If told to evacuate, go immediately
steps.body: A dam failure can send a wall of water downstream in minutes, and a levee breach can flood a neighborhood very fast. When ordered to leave, take only your go-bag, medicines, documents, and pets. If there is time and it is safe, turn off gas, electricity, and water and unplug appliances. Fill the car's tank only if you can do it without delay. Follow the posted evacuation route and expect heavy traffic. Do not stay behind to sandbag or move belongings. If you are not ordered to leave but are near the risk area, stay tuned and be ready to go.

steps.title: If water is coming, get high fast
steps.body: If you see or hear water rushing toward you, do not wait for an order. Move to higher ground immediately, going away from the river channel, not along it. Never walk or drive through floodwater - six inches (15 cm) of moving water can knock you down and stall or float a car. If you are trapped in a building, go to the highest floor, but not a closed attic, and onto the roof only if you must. Call 911 and signal for help with a bright cloth or flashlight.

steps.title: After a failure
steps.body: Return only when officials say it is safe. Floodwaters from a dam or levee break can stay high for days or weeks, and more failures may follow. Avoid floodwater, which may be contaminated, electrified, or deeper than it looks. Stay off flood-weakened roads and bridges and away from downed lines. Enter buildings slowly and carefully, since damage may be hidden. Check news reports to see if your water supply is safe before drinking it. Clean and disinfect everything floodwater touched, throw out food that touched it, and discard porous items that stayed wet more than 48 hours. Photograph damage for insurance and aid claims.

warnings: A levee lowers flood risk but does not remove it. Levees can be overtopped or breach without much warning.
Do not stay behind to sandbag or save belongings when told to evacuate from a dam or levee threat.
Never walk or drive through floodwater. Six inches (15 cm) of moving water can knock you down.
Do not go into a closed attic to escape rising water.
proTips: Drive your evacuation route during a dry day and note where the land rises above the flood area.
Ask your emergency manager what the siren or alert tone for a dam emergency sounds like where you live.
If you live behind a levee, find out who maintains it and whether it has had recent inspection issues.
Store copies of your flood policy and home photos in the cloud and in your go-bag.
source: FEMA / USACE / Fairfax County OEM / Ready Marine Corps
