whenNotTo: Do not try to inspect or repair a leaking dam or levee yourself. Report it and get away.
Do not evacuate toward the river or through low ground to reach your car if water is already coming - go up instead.

quickGlance.situation: A dam or levee near you is failing, overtopping, or under an emergency warning.
immediate: Leave right away if ordered - take only your go-bag, meds, and pets
If water is rushing toward you, go to higher ground now, away from the channel
Never walk or drive into floodwater
then: Stay out until officials say it is safe; more failures may follow
Treat floodwater as contaminated and electrified during cleanup

title: Severe Thunderstorms, Lightning, Derechos, and Hail
summary: Get indoors at the first rumble of thunder, understand what severe thunderstorm warnings mean, and protect yourself from damaging winds, derechos, and large hail.

steps.title: Understand severe thunderstorm alerts
steps.body: A Severe Thunderstorm Watch means conditions are right for severe storms - stay alert. A Severe Thunderstorm Warning means a storm is producing, or about to produce, hail 1 inch (2.5 cm) or larger and/or winds of 58 mph (93 km/h) or more. Since 2021 the NWS adds damage threat tags. 'Considerable' means hail at least 1.75 inches (4.4 cm) or winds at least 70 mph (113 km/h). 'Destructive' means hail at least 2.75 inches (7 cm) or winds at least 80 mph (129 km/h), and it sets off a Wireless Emergency Alert on phones. Treat a destructive warning like a tornado warning. Warnings do not cover lightning - every thunderstorm has dangerous lightning.

steps.title: When thunder roars, go indoors
steps.body: Lightning can strike 10 miles (16 km) or more from the rain, often before the storm arrives or after it seems to have passed. If you can hear thunder, you are close enough to be struck, even under clear sky. At the first rumble, go into a fully enclosed building with wiring and plumbing, or a hard-topped metal car or truck with the windows up. Sheds, picnic shelters, tents, dugouts, porches, and beach umbrellas do not protect you. Stay inside until 30 minutes after the last thunder you hear. Check the forecast before outdoor plans and have a shelter plan with enough time to reach it.

steps.title: Stay safe inside during lightning
steps.body: Lightning can travel through wiring, plumbing, and metal. During a storm, stay off corded phones (cell and cordless phones are fine). Avoid using electrical equipment plugged into the wall, and unplug electronics before the storm if you can - not during it. Do not shower, bathe, or wash dishes. Stay away from windows, doors, and porches, and do not lie on concrete floors or lean on concrete walls, which may have metal inside. Surge protectors help protect electronics but will not stop a direct strike.

steps.title: If you are caught outside with no shelter
steps.body: There is no truly safe place outdoors in a thunderstorm, so the goal is to lower your risk while you keep moving toward shelter. Get off ridges, hilltops, and open fields. Do not be the tallest object, and stay away from lone trees, towers, and poles. Get out of and away from water. Keep away from wire fences, power lines, and metal rails - metal does not attract lightning, but it carries current a long way. If you are in a group, spread out at least 50 feet (15 m) apart so one strike does not hit everyone. Keep heading to a building or car.

steps.title: Help someone struck by lightning
steps.body: Call 911 right away. Lightning victims do not carry an electrical charge, so it is safe to touch them. If the storm is still going, move the person and yourself to a safer spot if you can, since lightning can strike the same place twice. Check breathing. If they are not breathing normally, start CPR and use an AED as soon as one is available. Many lightning victims survive with fast CPR. Even people who seem fine should see a doctor, since lightning can cause burns, hearing loss, and nerve and heart problems that show up later.

steps.title: Brace for damaging winds and derechos
steps.body: Straight-line winds from thunderstorms can be as strong as a tornado. A derecho is a long-lived windstorm from a fast-moving line of storms, with a damage path at least 400 miles (650 km) long and 60 miles (100 km) wide, gusts of at least 58 mph (93 km/h) along most of it, and several gusts of 75 mph (121 km/h) or more. These storms can move 50 to 70 mph (80 to 113 km/h), so warning time is short. When a damaging wind warning is issued, go to an interior room on the lowest floor, away from windows - the same place you would use for a tornado. Falling trees are the main killer, so stay out of forests, tents, and cars parked under trees. Mobile homes, barns, and tents offer little protection. Get off lakes and the ocean early.

steps.title: Protect yourself from hail
steps.body: Large hail can break windows, damage roofs and cars, and badly injure people and animals. Get indoors and stay away from skylights and windows. If you are driving, pull over somewhere safe - under a gas station canopy or in a parking garage if you can reach it, but never under an overpass where you block traffic. Stay in the car, turn your back to the windows, and cover your head and eyes with a coat or blanket. Bring pets and livestock under cover before the storm. Move cars into a garage when large hail is forecast.

steps.title: After the storm
steps.body: Expect long power outages after derechos and big wind storms - sometimes for days. Stay far from downed or hanging power lines and report them. Watch for broken branches still hanging in trees. Use generators only outdoors, at least 20 feet (6 m) from openings. Be careful with chainsaws and ladders, and work with a partner. Check on neighbors, especially older adults during heat after a summer derecho. Photograph hail and wind damage for insurance, and be wary of door-to-door roofers asking for payment up front.

warnings: If you can hear thunder, you can be struck. Get inside a building or hard-topped car right away.
Picnic shelters, tents, sheds, and porches do not protect you from lightning.
Derecho winds can match a tornado. Shelter in an interior room on the lowest floor.
Never shelter from hail under a highway overpass - it blocks traffic and exposes you to wind.
Treat all downed power lines as live.
proTips: Use the 30-minute rule: reset your timer every time you hear thunder before going back out.
Organized outdoor events should have a written lightning plan with a set shelter and someone in charge of calling it.
Keep a cheap moving blanket in the car to cover yourself and the glass during hail.
Plug electronics into surge protectors before storm season so you do not need to unplug during a storm.

sources.title: New Damage Threat Categories for Severe Thunderstorm Warnings

whenNotTo: Do not stay outside to finish a game, hike, or chore once you hear thunder.
Do not rely on rubber tires or rubber shoes for lightning protection - a hard metal roof and body are what protect you in a car.

quickGlance.situation: A thunderstorm is coming, you hear thunder, or a Severe Thunderstorm Warning is issued.
immediate: Go inside a building or hard-topped car at the first thunder
For a destructive wind warning, go to an interior room on the lowest floor
Stay off corded phones, showers, and plugged-in electronics
then: Wait 30 minutes after the last thunder before going out
If someone is struck, call 911 and start CPR if they are not breathing - they are safe to touch

title: Solar Storms (Geomagnetic Storms) - What They Can and Can't Do
summary: Separate fact from fear about solar storms: understand NOAA's G1-G5 scale, which systems a severe storm can disrupt, what it will not do to you or your phone, and the simple steps that cover the real risks.

steps.title: Know what a solar storm is
steps.body: The Sun sends out bursts of energy. Solar flares are flashes of radiation that reach Earth in about 8 minutes and can black out high-frequency (HF) radio on the daylit side of the planet. Coronal mass ejections (CMEs) are huge clouds of charged gas that take roughly 1 to 4 days to arrive. When a CME hits Earth's magnetic field, it can cause a geomagnetic storm - often called a solar storm. NOAA's Space Weather Prediction Center (SWPC) watches the Sun around the clock and issues watches, warnings, and alerts, usually with a day or more of notice for CME-driven storms.

steps.title: Read the NOAA G-scale
steps.body: SWPC rates geomagnetic storms from G1 (minor) to G5 (extreme). G1 storms bring weak power grid swings and aurora at high latitudes and happen hundreds of times in an 11-year solar cycle. G3 (strong) can trigger false alarms on grid equipment and cause on-and-off GPS and HF radio problems. G4 (severe) can cause widespread voltage control problems and degrade satellite navigation for hours; it happens about 100 times per cycle. G5 (extreme) happens only a handful of times per cycle. It can cause blackouts, damage transformers, make HF radio impossible in many areas for 1-2 days, and degrade satellite navigation for days. SWPC also has an R-scale for radio blackouts and an S-scale for radiation storms.

steps.title: Know what a severe storm can disrupt
steps.body: The main risks are to big systems. Long power lines can pick up extra currents that strain transformers and protection systems, which can lead to outages. In March 1989 a storm knocked out the Quebec power grid, leaving about 6 million people in the dark for about 9 hours. GPS can lose accuracy or drop out, which affects navigation, surveying, precision farming, and some timing systems. HF radio, used by aircraft, ships, ham operators, and emergency teams, can fade or go silent. Satellites can be damaged or drift, and airline crews and passengers on polar routes get extra radiation. In May 2024, the first G5 storm since 2003 reached Earth; grid operators took precautions and the U.S. avoided major blackouts, but GPS and radio users saw problems.

steps.title: Know what a solar storm will not do
steps.body: A geomagnetic storm is not dangerous to people on the ground - Earth's atmosphere and magnetic field shield you from the radiation. It does not fry phones, laptops, cars, or small electronics the way a nuclear electromagnetic pulse (EMP) might; the currents build up in very long conductors like power lines and pipelines, not in a phone or a car. You do not need to unplug everything, hide indoors, or wrap devices in foil. Cell phones may still work, but service can drop if the power grid fails or GPS timing is affected. Be skeptical of viral posts that claim a storm will cause days of 'internet blackout' worldwide - check SWPC instead.

steps.title: Prepare the way you would for any outage
steps.body: The real household risk from an extreme storm is a power outage, possibly a long one if transformers are damaged. The same basic kit covers it: water, food, medicines, flashlights, batteries, a battery or hand-crank radio, a way to charge phones, and a plan for heating or cooling. Keep a paper map and know your routes in case GPS is unreliable. If you depend on powered medical equipment, have a backup power plan and register with your utility. Keep some cash in case card systems are down. If you use HF radio, expect poor conditions and have VHF/UHF or other backups.

steps.title: Follow alerts and enjoy the aurora
steps.body: Sign up for SWPC's free email alerts or check its website and social feeds for watches (storm expected), warnings (storm imminent), and alerts (storm under way). Local news and your utility will share any grid concerns. During strong storms the aurora may be visible much farther south than usual - G4 storms can reach about Alabama and northern California, and G5 storms as far as Florida and south Texas. Go somewhere dark, look north, and use your phone camera, which often picks up color your eyes miss. Watch your footing and traffic when you go out at night to look.

warnings: Do not confuse a solar storm with a nuclear EMP. A solar storm mainly affects long power lines, satellites, GPS, and HF radio - not personal electronics.
An extreme (G5) storm could cause long power outages if transformers are damaged. Keep outage supplies ready.
GPS may be inaccurate during strong storms. Do not rely on it alone for navigation in remote areas.
Ignore viral claims that are not backed by NOAA SWPC.
proTips: Sign up for SWPC email alerts - it is free and gives you hours to days of notice.
Keep a printed road map and a compass in the car as a GPS backup.
Ham operators: G-storms often improve some VHF propagation at high latitudes even as HF fades.
The SWPC aurora dashboard shows a 30-minute aurora forecast for your area.
source: NOAA Space Weather Prediction Center / NWS / USGS Geomagnetism Program
whenNotTo: Do not unplug or shield all your electronics for a solar storm - it is not needed for personal devices.
Do not treat a G1-G3 storm as an emergency for your household; it rarely affects daily life.

quickGlance.situation: NOAA SWPC has issued a geomagnetic storm watch or warning, or the news is talking about a big solar storm.
immediate: Check the storm level (G1-G5) at NOAA SWPC, not social media
Make sure outage basics are ready: water, lights, radio, phone charging
Do not rely on GPS alone if you are traveling in remote areas
then: Follow your utility for any grid notices
Go outside after dark and look north for the aurora

title: Pandemics and Disease Outbreaks - Household Preparation and Isolation
summary: How to prepare your household for a serious disease outbreak, lower the chance of spreading illness at home, and care for a sick family member while keeping everyone else well.

steps.title: Stock up gradually, before the rush
steps.body: Ready.gov advises keeping several days to several weeks of supplies, bought a little at a time so stores are not stripped bare. Aim for at least two weeks of shelf-stable food and water, a 30-day supply of prescriptions if your insurer allows refills early, fever reducers and other over-the-counter medicines, a thermometer, soap, alcohol-based hand sanitizer (at least 60% alcohol), household cleaner, disposable gloves, tissues, trash bags, and well-fitting masks. Add oral rehydration salts for vomiting or diarrhea. Rotate food and medicine so nothing expires.

steps.title: Plan for closures and a sick adult
steps.body: Outbreaks close schools, offices, and day care. Talk to your employer about telework and sick leave. Arrange backup child care and decide who cares for children if both parents are ill. Review your health insurance, including telehealth visits. Keep a written list of each person's medicines, allergies, doctors, and pharmacy. Store password-protected digital copies of key documents. Pick a friend or neighbor who can drop off groceries or medicine at your door, and offer to do the same for them.

steps.title: Use the core prevention habits
steps.body: Stay up to date on vaccines for flu, COVID-19, and RSV if you are eligible, and on any vaccine officials offer for a new outbreak. Wash hands with soap and water for at least 20 seconds, especially after coughing, using the bathroom, and before eating; use sanitizer when soap is not available. Cover coughs and sneezes with a tissue or your elbow. Clean frequently touched surfaces like doorknobs, faucets, phones, and remotes. Bring in fresh air by opening windows or using a portable air purifier, and gather outdoors when you can. Wear a mask in crowded indoor places when officials advise it.

steps.title: Stay home when sick
steps.body: CDC's current respiratory virus guidance (updated March 2024) says to stay home and away from others when you are sick. You can return to normal activities when, for at least 24 hours, your symptoms are improving overall and any fever has been gone without fever-reducing medicine. For the next 5 days, take extra care: wear a mask around others, keep distance, wash hands often, and improve indoor air. This replaced the older fixed 5-day isolation rule for COVID-19. During a new or severe outbreak, health officials may give stricter rules; follow the latest instructions from your state or local health department.

steps.title: Set up a sick room at home
steps.body: Keep the sick person in one room with the door closed, and if possible use a separate bathroom. Choose one healthy adult to be the caregiver, ideally someone not at high risk. Open a window or run a fan pointed out the window to move air outside. Both the patient and caregiver should wear masks when together. Give the patient their own cup, towels, and utensils, and wash dishes and laundry in hot water. The caregiver should wash hands after every contact. Clean shared bathroom surfaces daily.

steps.title: Watch for warning signs
steps.body: Check the sick person at least twice a day: temperature, how much they drink, how often they urinate, and how hard they breathe. Call a doctor or telehealth service early if they are older, pregnant, very young, or have a chronic illness; some antiviral medicines work best in the first days. Call 911 for trouble breathing, chest pain or pressure, new confusion, inability to stay awake, bluish lips or face, or signs of severe dehydration such as no urine for many hours. Tell the dispatcher about the illness so responders can protect themselves.

steps.title: Protect your mind and your community
steps.body: Long outbreaks are stressful and lonely. Keep routines, stay connected by phone and video, and limit how much news you watch. Share only accurate information from health officials; false cures and rumors cause real harm. Do not blame or shame groups of people for the disease. Watch for scams selling fake tests, cures, or 'government relief.' If you feel overwhelmed, the Disaster Distress Helpline (call or text 1-800-985-5990) is open 24/7.

warnings: Never take antibiotics, antivirals, or other prescription drugs that were not prescribed to you. They will not help most viral illness and can cause serious harm.
Do not give aspirin to children or teens with fever or flu-like illness; follow the label on any fever reducer.
Hoarding medicine and supplies at the last minute creates shortages for people who need them most - build your supply early and gradually.
Severe breathing trouble is an emergency. Do not wait for a telehealth callback - call 911.
proTips: Keep a simple log in the sick room: time, temperature, fluids taken, medicine given (per label), and symptoms. It helps doctors and prevents double-dosing.
A box fan with a furnace filter strapped to it is a low-cost room air cleaner many health agencies have described for smoke and germs.
Pre-pack a 'sick kit' bin: thermometer, masks, gloves, tissues, trash bags, electrolyte powder, and a printed medication list.
Agree with a neighbor on a 'porch drop' system so groceries and medicine arrive without face-to-face contact.

sources.title: CDC updates and simplifies respiratory virus recommendations
Safety Guidelines: Returning Home After a Natural Disaster (Disaster Distress Helpline)

whenNotTo: Do not rely on home isolation alone for someone with emergency warning signs - get medical care.
Do not follow generic return-to-normal timelines if your health department issues stricter rules for a specific outbreak.

quickGlance.situation: A serious disease outbreak is spreading in your area or someone at home is sick.
immediate: Keep the sick person in one room with a closed door and masks when together
Wash hands 20 seconds; clean shared surfaces daily
Watch for trouble breathing, chest pain, confusion, bluish lips - call 911
then: Return to normal only after 24 hours improving and fever-free without medicine
Take extra precautions for 5 more days; follow local health department rules

title: Chemical and Hazmat Releases - Shelter in Place or Evacuate
summary: What to do when a chemical spill, train derailment, plant leak, or toxic cloud threatens your area: how to choose between leaving and sheltering, and how to seal a room properly.

steps.title: Get the official instruction first
steps.body: Chemical releases move with the wind, and only officials with air monitoring know where the plume is going. Turn on a radio, TV, or phone alerts as soon as you hear sirens, see a strange cloud, or smell something odd. Officials will tell you either to evacuate or to shelter in place. Follow that order exactly. CDC says to shelter in place when leaving would be more dangerous than staying - for example, when the cloud is already passing over or roads would take you through it. If you are told to evacuate, leave right away by the route given.

steps.title: If you are outside, move away and get inside
steps.body: If you notice a chemical smell, eye or throat burning, coughing, or a visible cloud, move away from it at once. Try to go crosswind or upwind, away from the direction the cloud is drifting, and to higher ground if the gas seems to hug the ground. Cover your nose and mouth with cloth while you move, but know that cloth does not filter toxic gas. Get inside the nearest building. Cars are not airtight; if you must stay in a car, close windows and vents, turn off the fan and air conditioning, and listen for instructions.

steps.title: Choose the right room
steps.body: Bring everyone, including pets, inside. Close and lock all outside doors and windows. Pick a room you can seal that is large enough for everyone, has few or no windows, and has a water source if possible, like a large bathroom or master bedroom. CDC advises a room on the highest floor possible. Many toxic gases are heavier than air and collect in basements and low spots. Note that this is the opposite of radiation, where basements are best. Bring a phone and charger, a battery radio, water, medicines, and your go-kit.

steps.title: Shut off outside air
steps.body: Turn off the furnace, air conditioner, and all fans, including bathroom and kitchen exhaust fans and the clothes dryer. Close the fireplace damper. Cover window air conditioners. These systems pull outside air, and the chemical, into the house. If you have a whole-house fresh-air intake or a smart thermostat set to run the fan, switch it to off. Do this before you seal the room so you do not have to leave it later.

steps.title: Seal the room
steps.body: Once inside the room, close the door. Tape plastic sheeting over windows and vents, overlapping the edges and taping all four sides flat. Tape around the door frame and lay a wet towel along the gap under the door. If you have no plastic, stuff towels, sheets, or clothing into vents and gaps. Pre-cut 2-4 mil plastic sheets labeled for each window make this take minutes instead of a half hour. A sealed room is meant for a few hours, not days; the air inside will slowly get stale, so listen for the all-clear.

steps.title: Wait for the all-clear, then air out
steps.body: CDC says you may need to stay put for a few hours, possibly longer. Keep listening to the radio. Do not leave until police, fire, or other officials announce it is safe. Then open windows and doors, turn the HVAC back on, and go outside to fresh air while the house airs out. Follow any extra instructions about cleaning surfaces, garden produce, or pets. If you start to feel sick inside the sealed room - headache, dizziness, coughing - call 911 and tell them where you are sheltering.

steps.title: Decontaminate if you were exposed
steps.body: If a chemical touched your skin or clothes, remove clothing quickly; cut off shirts rather than pulling them over your face. Put them in a sealed plastic bag. Wash skin with plenty of soap and water, and flush eyes with clean water for at least 10-15 minutes, removing contact lenses first. Do not scrub hard. Put on clean clothes. Call 911 or Poison Control (1-800-222-1222) and tell them what the chemical might be. Seek medical care for any breathing trouble, burns, or eye pain.

warnings: Do not drive into or through a visible cloud or strong chemical smell to 'get out faster.' Turn around or get indoors.
Never shelter in a basement for a chemical release unless officials tell you to - many toxic gases sink and collect low.
A sealed room is for hours. Do not stay sealed for days without fresh air; follow official guidance.
Do not go back to pick up children from school; schools have their own shelter plans.
proTips: Pre-cut and label plastic sheets for your shelter room's windows and vents, and store them with duct tape, scissors, and towels.
Practice sealing the room once with your family - it reveals missing supplies and saves time in a real event.
If you live near rail lines, highways, or chemical plants, sign up for county alerts and learn the local siren signals.
Keep a battery radio in the shelter room so you do not need to leave it to hear updates.

sources.title: What to Do to Shelter in Place for a Chemical Emergency
What to Do: Get Inside (radiation - for contrast on room choice)

whenNotTo: Do not shelter in place if officials order an evacuation, or if the building itself is on fire or filling with fumes.
Do not seal a room while running any fuel-burning heater, stove, or generator - carbon monoxide will build up fast.

quickGlance.situation: Sirens, an alert, a strange cloud, or a chemical smell signal a hazardous materials release nearby.
immediate: Get inside; bring people and pets; close and lock doors and windows
Turn off HVAC, all fans, dryer; close fireplace damper
Go to an upper-floor room with few windows and seal it with plastic and tape
then: Listen to a radio and wait for the official all-clear, then air out
If exposed, remove clothing, wash with soap and water, call 911 or Poison Control

title: House Fire - Smoke Alarms, Two Ways Out, and Escaping Fast
summary: Set up working smoke alarms and a practiced escape plan with two ways out of every room, and know exactly what to do in the first minutes of a home fire.

steps.title: Install smoke alarms in the right places
steps.body: The U.S. Fire Administration says to put smoke alarms on every level of the home, including the basement, both inside and outside sleeping areas. That means one in each bedroom and one in the hallway outside them. Mount them on the ceiling or high on the wall, and keep them about 10 feet (3 m) from the stove to cut nuisance alarms. Interconnected alarms, where one sounds and all sound, give everyone the most warning. For anyone who is deaf or hard of hearing, add alarms with strobe lights or bed shakers.

steps.title: Test monthly, replace at 10 years
steps.body: Press the test button on every alarm once a month. Replace any alarm that is 10 years old or older; the date is printed on the back. If an alarm chirps, replace the battery or the whole unit right away. Never take the battery out to stop cooking alarms - fan the air or open a window instead. Also install carbon monoxide alarms on each level and test them monthly. In a grid-down period, fire risk goes up from candles, heaters, and generators, so check alarms have working batteries.

steps.title: Map two ways out of every room
steps.body: Draw a simple floor plan of your home showing every door and window. Mark two exits from each room, usually the door and a window. Make sure windows open easily, screens can be pushed out, and security bars have quick-release latches from inside. For second-floor bedrooms, keep an escape ladder near the window and practice setting it up. Keep hallways and exits clear of clutter. Make sure your house number is easy to see from the street so firefighters can find you.

steps.title: Pick a meeting place and practice twice a year
steps.body: Choose an outside meeting spot a safe distance in front of the home, such as a tree, light pole, or mailbox. Everyone goes straight there so you can count heads. Practice the plan at least twice a year with everyone in the home, including one drill at night with the lights off. Teach children to escape on their own and never to hide under beds or in closets. Assign an adult to help babies, older adults, or anyone with a disability. USFA warns a small flame can become a major fire in under 30 seconds, so the plan has to be automatic.

steps.title: When the alarm sounds, get out
steps.body: Yell 'Fire!' and leave at once. Do not stop for belongings, pets you cannot quickly grab, or phone calls. If there is smoke, get low and crawl under it, where the air is cleaner and cooler. Before opening a closed door, feel the knob and the door with the back of your hand. If it is hot, use your second way out. If it is cool, open it slowly and be ready to shut it if smoke or heat rushes in. Close doors behind you as you leave; a closed door slows the spread of fire and smoke.

steps.title: If you are trapped
steps.body: If both exits are blocked, stay in a room with a window and close the door. Stuff towels, sheets, or clothes in the gaps around the door and vents to keep smoke out. Call 911 and tell them exactly where you are. Open the window a little at the top for air if there is no smoke outside, and signal with a flashlight or a light-colored cloth. Stay low. If your clothes catch fire, stop where you are, drop to the ground, cover your face with your hands, and roll until the flames are out.

steps.title: Get out and stay out
steps.body: Once outside, go to the meeting place and call 911 from there with a cell phone or a neighbor's phone. Never go back inside a burning building for any reason, including people or pets; tell firefighters right away who may still be inside and where. Stay out until the fire department says it is safe. Afterward, do not use utilities until they have been checked, and contact your insurer and the Red Cross or local agencies for help with housing.

warnings: Never go back inside a burning home. Tell firefighters where missing people or pets might be.
Never disable a smoke alarm or borrow its battery for another device.
Do not use the elevator in an apartment building during a fire - use the stairs.
During power outages, candles, space heaters, and generators cause many home fires. Keep heat sources 3 feet (1 m) from anything that can burn.
proTips: Close bedroom doors at night. A closed door can hold back smoke and heat long enough for you to escape through the window.
Keep shoes, glasses, a flashlight, and your phone by the bed.
Turn every daylight-saving time change into your reminder to test alarms and practice the drill.
Sealed 10-year battery alarms remove the yearly battery change and the temptation to pull batteries.
whenNotTo: Do not try to fight a fire that is spreading, between you and the exit, or bigger than a small wastebasket - get out.
Do not open a hot door to escape - use your second way out.

quickGlance.situation: Your smoke alarm is sounding or you see smoke or fire in your home.
immediate: Yell 'Fire!' and get out now - leave belongings
Crawl low under smoke; feel doors with the back of your hand
Use your second way out if a door is hot; close doors behind you
then: Go to the meeting place and call 911 from outside
Never go back inside - tell firefighters who is missing

title: Explosions, Attacks, and Building Collapse - Immediate Actions
summary: What to do in the first minutes after an explosion, attack in a public place, or building collapse: take cover, get out safely, watch for a second attack, signal if trapped, and help others without becoming a victim.

steps.title: Take cover first
steps.body: When an explosion happens or things start falling, get under a sturdy table or desk, or against an inside wall away from windows, and protect your head and neck. Stay put until debris stops falling. Flying glass and falling objects cause many of the injuries. Stay calm and look around before you move: check for fire, smoke, cracked or sagging ceilings, and damaged stairways. Ready.gov notes emergency services may not arrive right away, so the next minutes are up to you and the people around you.

steps.title: Get out quickly and safely
steps.body: If it is safe, leave the building right away. Do not stop to collect belongings or make phone calls. Use stairs, never elevators. Stay low if there is smoke. Avoid floors and stairways that look weak, cracked, or sagging, and stay away from damaged walls on the way out. Once outside, keep moving away from the building and from glass facades that could still fall. Do not gather in front of the building or in a parking lot right next to it.

steps.title: Watch for a second attack
steps.body: Attackers sometimes plan a second device or assault aimed at crowds and responders. CISA advises staying alert for secondary attacks after you call 911. Move well away from the scene, avoid crowds, and do not touch or move unattended bags, packages, or vehicles. Report anything suspicious to police. Do not stay to film. If you hear gunfire, use run, hide, fight: run to the nearest safe exit if you can; if not, hide in a room you can lock or barricade and silence your phone; fight only as a last resort when your life is in immediate danger.

steps.title: If you are trapped under debris
steps.body: Do not light a match or lighter; there may be gas leaks. Cover your nose and mouth with cloth to filter dust. Move as little as possible so you do not kick up dust or shift debris. Signal rescuers by tapping on a pipe or wall, blowing a whistle, or shining a flashlight. Ready.gov says to shout only as a last resort, because shouting makes you breathe in dangerous dust. Text 911 or a contact if your phone works and save battery between tries. Pace your energy; rescues can take hours.

steps.title: Call for help and help others safely
steps.body: Once you are safe, call 911 and describe the location, what happened, and the number of injured. Bystanders are often the first help. Help walking wounded move away from the scene. Control heavy bleeding with firm pressure or a tourniquet if you are trained. Use simple triage: help the people who are not breathing well or bleeding heavily first. Ready.gov warns not to try to dig out people who are trapped under debris you cannot safely move, because shifting rubble can kill them or you; tell rescuers exactly where they are when crews arrive.

steps.title: Follow responders and stay informed
steps.body: When police arrive, keep your hands empty and visible, follow their commands, and do not run toward them or grab them. They may treat everyone as a possible threat at first. Tell them what you saw. Let your family know you are safe with a text or a social media post; save voice calls for emergencies so networks stay open. Keep listening to officials, even if you were not near the scene, since you may be told to evacuate an area or shut off utilities.

steps.title: Prepare before it happens
steps.body: In any building you visit often, notice two exits. Keep a small flashlight, whistle, and dust mask in your bag. Make sure your employer has your emergency contacts and any medical needs. Learn bleeding control and CPR. Report suspicious activity to local police: 'If you see something, say something.' After any attack, expect strong stress reactions; talk with others and get support if sleep, appetite, or mood are affected for weeks.

warnings: Never use elevators after an explosion or during a fire.
Do not light matches or lighters if trapped - gas may be leaking.
Do not try to pull people out from under heavy debris yourself; mark their location and tell rescuers.
Do not touch unattended packages or vehicles near the scene - a second device is possible.
proTips: A whistle on your keychain is the best low-cost signaling tool if you are ever trapped.
Keep your phone on low-power mode and text instead of calling to stretch battery and network capacity.
When police arrive, show empty hands and follow commands - fast movement toward officers can be mistaken for a threat.
Take a 'Stop the Bleed' or first aid course; bystanders with training save lives before ambulances can reach the scene.
whenNotTo: Do not leave a secure hiding place during an active attack just because the noise stopped - wait for police instructions.
Do not re-enter a damaged building to retrieve belongings or search for people.

quickGlance.situation: An explosion, attack, or collapse just happened where you are.
immediate: Take cover under something sturdy until debris stops falling
Leave by stairs if safe; stay low in smoke; never use elevators
Move far away and watch for a second attack
If trapped: cover mouth, tap or whistle, shout only as last resort
then: Call 911; help the injured only where it is safe
Show empty hands and follow police commands; text family

title: Extended Regional Power Outage - The First 72 Hours and the First Two Weeks
summary: A timeline for a long, widespread blackout: what to do in the first hours, how to get through the first three days safely, and how to run your household for two weeks without grid power.

steps.title: First hour: check, report, and protect
steps.body: Look outside to see if neighbors are also dark, and report the outage to your utility. Switch off or unplug appliances and electronics, leaving one lamp on so you know when power returns; this protects them from the surge. Fill bottles, pots, and the bathtub with tap water, since water pressure may drop if pumps lose power. Charge phones and power banks from a car or battery while you can. Get flashlights out and put candles away; they are a leading cause of outage fires.

steps.title: Keep the cold in
steps.body: Keep fridge and freezer doors closed. FoodSafety.gov says a closed refrigerator keeps food safe for about 4 hours. A full freezer holds for about 48 hours, a half-full one about 24 hours. Put an appliance thermometer in each; the fridge must stay at 40 F (4 C) or below and the freezer at 0 F (-18 C). After 4 hours without power, move perishables like meat, milk, and leftovers to a cooler with ice. Block or dry ice can stretch the freezer; about 50 pounds of dry ice keeps an 18-cubic-foot freezer cold for about 2 days. Never touch dry ice bare-handed.

steps.title: Prevent carbon monoxide poisoning
steps.body: Carbon monoxide (CO) is the top killer in long outages. Run generators, camp stoves, and grills only outdoors, at least 20 feet (6 m) from windows, doors, and vents. Never use a gas oven or stove to heat the home. Never run a car in a garage, even with the door open. Put battery-powered CO alarms on every level and near bedrooms. Headache, dizziness, nausea, and confusion that improve when you go outside are warning signs; get everyone into fresh air and call 911. Never connect a generator to house wiring without a proper transfer switch; it can kill utility workers.

steps.title: Days 1-3: medicine, heat, and cold
steps.body: Replace refrigerated medicines like insulin if the power has been out a day or more, unless the label says otherwise, and ask a pharmacist about anything that got warm. If someone depends on oxygen, a CPAP, dialysis, or other powered equipment, use backup batteries and contact the provider or 911 early. In heat, stay in the coolest room, drink water often, and go to a cooling center if one opens. In cold, close off unused rooms, dress in layers, and sleep together in one room. Check on older neighbors twice a day.

steps.title: Days 1-3: food, water, and sanitation
steps.body: Eat food from the fridge first, then the freezer, then shelf-stable items. When in doubt, throw it out; never taste food to test it. Plan on at least 1 gallon (about 4 liters) of water per person per day for drinking and basic hygiene. If your water utility issues a boil notice, follow it. If toilets will not flush, pour a bucket of water into the bowl to flush, or set up a bag-lined bucket toilet with a lid. Keep hands clean with soap and stored water or sanitizer, especially before eating.

steps.title: Days 4-14: settle into a routine
steps.body: A two-week outage means scheduling. Run a generator in short blocks to chill the fridge, charge batteries, and pump water, rather than nonstop, to stretch fuel. Store fuel safely outside the living space. Keep a daily routine for meals, water treatment, trash, and sleep. Bag and seal garbage, and keep it away from the house to avoid pests. Expect gas stations, ATMs, and card readers to fail, so keep some cash in small bills. Use a battery or hand-crank radio for news, and set times to check in with neighbors and family.

steps.title: When power comes back
steps.body: Turn appliances back on a few at a time to avoid overloading circuits. Check the fridge and freezer thermometers. Discard any perishable food that sat above 40 F for more than 4 hours, and anything that smells, looks, or feels off. Refill and rotate your water and food storage. Replace refrigerated medicines that warmed. Write down what ran out first and what you wished you had, and fix those gaps before the next outage.

warnings: Never run a generator, grill, or camp stove indoors, in a garage, or near open windows. CO can kill in minutes.
Do not back-feed a generator into your house wiring without a transfer switch - it is illegal and can electrocute line workers.
Stay well away from downed power lines and anything touching them, and assume they are live. Call the utility or 911.
Do not store food outdoors or in snow; sun and animals make it unsafe.
proTips: Freeze water bottles now to fill empty freezer space; full freezers stay cold longer and the ice doubles as drinking water.
Register anyone who uses powered medical equipment with your utility's medical priority program if one exists.
A small solar panel and power bank keep phones and radios running without fuel.
Keep a paper list of key phone numbers - your contacts are useless when the phone is dead.

whenNotTo: Do not stay home without power if someone needs life-sustaining powered equipment and backup batteries are running low - go to a hospital or shelter.
Do not ride out extreme heat or cold at home if indoor temperatures become dangerous - go to a cooling or warming center.

quickGlance.situation: A widespread blackout may last days or weeks.
immediate: Unplug electronics; leave one lamp on to know when power returns
Fill containers with water; keep fridge and freezer closed
Use flashlights, not candles; generators outdoors only, 20+ feet away
then: Move perishables to a cooler after 4 hours; replace warmed refrigerated medicine
Set a daily routine for water, food, sanitation, and neighbor check-ins

title: Cyberattacks and Financial System Outages - Cash, Records, and Payments
summary: How to keep paying for essentials and protect your money and identity when a cyberattack, ransomware event, or payment system outage knocks out cards, ATMs, banking apps, or online services.

steps.title: Keep emergency cash at home
steps.body: Ready.gov advises keeping a small amount of cash at home in a safe place, in small bills, because ATMs and card readers may not work after a disaster or cyber incident. A common household target is enough to cover one to two weeks of essentials like food, fuel, and medicine; set an amount that fits your budget. Store it in a fire-resistant box or safe, out of sight, and do not tell people outside your household where it is. Include coins and small bills, since stores without power or networks may not be able to make change.

steps.title: Build a paper and digital records kit
steps.body: Gather copies of photo IDs, birth certificates, Social Security cards, military records, insurance policies, deeds or leases, recent tax returns, and pay stubs. Add medical records, medication lists, and immunization records. Write down account numbers and the phone numbers for your banks, card issuers, insurers, and utilities, since you cannot look them up when sites are down. Ready.gov suggests storing copies in a safe deposit box, on an encrypted external drive, or in secure cloud storage. Keep the original papers in a waterproof, fire-resistant container you can grab in an evacuation.

steps.title: Harden your accounts now
steps.body: CISA's Secure Our World program lists four basics. Use long, unique passwords for every account and keep them in a password manager. Turn on multifactor authentication (MFA) for email, banking, and shopping accounts; this alone blocks most account takeovers. Install software updates on your phone, computer, and router as soon as they come out. Learn to spot phishing: unexpected messages that pressure you to click a link, open an attachment, or share a code. Write down MFA recovery codes and keep them with your records kit.

steps.title: Spread your risk
steps.body: Do not rely on one bank, one card, or one payment app. Keep at least two ways to pay, such as a debit card and a credit card from different banks, plus cash. Know your bank's branch locations and hours in case online banking fails. Keep a few paper checks. Back up important files on an external drive that you unplug after each backup so ransomware cannot reach it. Keep your phone charged and a power bank ready; many banks use texted codes to verify you.

steps.title: During an outage, verify and stay calm
steps.body: When cards, ATMs, or bank apps fail, check your bank's official status page or call the number on the back of your card. Do not use links in texts, emails, or social posts claiming to fix the problem. Scammers move fast during outages, posing as banks, utilities, or government agencies. No real bank will ask you to read back a one-time code or move money to a 'safe account.' Pay with cash for essentials, keep receipts, and avoid large purchases until systems are back and you can confirm charges.

steps.title: If you are hacked or your data is stolen
steps.body: Disconnect the infected device from the internet. From a different, clean device, change passwords for email first, then banking and other accounts, and turn on MFA. Call your bank and card issuers to freeze or replace cards and flag suspicious charges. Place a free credit freeze with Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion. Report identity theft at IdentityTheft.gov and cyber crimes at the FBI's IC3.gov. Keep notes of every call, date, and reference number.

steps.title: Watch your accounts after it ends
steps.body: After a breach or a long outage, check bank and card statements weekly for several months, since stolen data can be used much later. Pull your free credit reports from AnnualCreditReport.com. Expect delayed deposits or doubled charges when payment systems recover, and dispute errors in writing. Refill your cash reserve and update your records kit with anything you found missing during the outage.

warnings: Never share a one-time passcode, password, or PIN with anyone who contacts you, even if they claim to be your bank or the government.
Keep cash hidden and private. Large visible amounts make you a target, especially during wider disasters.
Do not plug in USB drives or open attachments you were not expecting, especially during a known cyber incident.
Do not pay ransomware demands on a personal device; disconnect it and get trusted help instead.
proTips: Write a one-page 'money card' with each account's institution, last four digits, and fraud phone number, and keep it with your cash.
Set up account alerts by text or email for every charge so fraud shows up fast.
Ready.gov points to the Emergency Financial First Aid Kit (EFFAK), a free FEMA and Operation HOPE workbook for organizing records.
A prepaid phone plan or second SIM can keep you reachable for bank verification if your main carrier is down.

sources.title: Secure Yourself and Your Family (Secure Our World)

whenNotTo: Do not pull all your savings out of the bank in a panic during a short outage - it raises theft risk and your deposits remain insured.
Do not use public Wi-Fi to log into banking during an incident if you can avoid it.

quickGlance.situation: Cards, ATMs, banking apps, or online services are down because of a cyberattack or system outage.
immediate: Pay for essentials with cash in small bills
Check status only through official bank sites or the number on your card
Ignore texts and calls offering to 'fix' your account; never share codes
then: If hacked: disconnect, change passwords from a clean device, call your bank
Freeze credit and report at IdentityTheft.gov and IC3.gov

title: Boil-Water Notices and Municipal Water System Failures
summary: What a boil-water notice means, how to make tap water safe by boiling or bleach, what you can and cannot use tap water for, and what to do when the notice is lifted or the water stops entirely.

steps.title: Know which notice you are under
steps.body: A boil-water advisory or notice means germs such as bacteria, viruses, or parasites may be in the tap water, often after a main break, pressure loss, flooding, or treatment failure. Boiling kills them. A 'do not drink' or 'do not use' notice is different: it usually means a chemical problem, and boiling will not help and can even concentrate some chemicals. Read the exact wording from your water utility or health department, and follow it. Sign up for your utility's text or email alerts so you hear about notices fast.

steps.title: Boil water the right way
steps.body: If the water is cloudy, let it settle and pour it through a clean cloth, paper towel, or coffee filter first. Bring the water to a full rolling boil for 1 minute. CDC says to boil for 3 minutes above 6,500 feet; EPA's page uses a lower altitude cutoff, so if you live above 5,000 feet (1,500 m), boil for 3 minutes to be safe. Let it cool on its own, then store it in clean, covered containers. Add a pinch of salt or pour it back and forth between two clean containers to improve the flat taste.

steps.title: Use bleach if you cannot boil
steps.body: If you have no way to boil, EPA says you can disinfect clear water with plain, unscented household bleach. For 6% bleach, add 8 drops per gallon (about 4 liters). For 8.25% bleach, add 6 drops per gallon. Double the dose if the water is cloudy, colored, or very cold. Stir and wait 30 minutes. The water should have a slight chlorine smell; if not, repeat the dose and wait 15 more minutes. Do not use scented, color-safe, or 'splashless' bleach. Bleach does not remove chemicals or kill all parasites as well as boiling does.

steps.title: Know what needs safe water
steps.body: Use boiled or bottled water for drinking, cooking, making ice, brushing teeth, washing fruits and vegetables, and mixing baby formula or juice. Throw out ice made during the advisory. Pets should drink safe water too. For hand washing, soap and tap water are usually fine unless officials say otherwise; use sanitizer after. Adults can shower or bathe but should not swallow water; give babies and young children a sponge bath. Use a dishwasher only if it has a hot or sanitizing cycle, or wash by hand and rinse in water with a small amount of bleach.

steps.title: When the water stops completely
steps.body: If taps run dry, turn to stored water first: plan on at least 1 gallon per person per day. Your water heater tank, the toilet tank (not the bowl), and ice cubes hold clean water you can use. Turn off the water heater's power or gas before draining it. Save water by using paper plates, hand sanitizer, and a bucket of water to flush the toilet only when needed. If you must use outside water from a rain barrel, stream, or pond, filter and disinfect it first.

steps.title: After the notice is lifted
steps.body: Wait for the official 'lift' announcement before using tap water normally. Then flush your plumbing: run all cold taps for several minutes until the water feels cold and clear, starting with the lowest floor. Run the water heater through a cycle or flush it if your utility recommends it. Throw out ice from the icemaker and run it through a few cycles. Replace water filters on fridges, pitchers, and under-sink units. Clean and refill pet bowls, and run an empty dishwasher cycle.

steps.title: Watch for illness
steps.body: Stomach cramps, diarrhea, vomiting, and fever days after the advisory may mean someone drank contaminated water. Keep them drinking safe fluids or oral rehydration solution. Call a doctor if symptoms last more than a couple of days, if there is blood in the stool, or if the person is very young, older, pregnant, or has a weak immune system. Tell the doctor about the water notice; it can change testing and treatment.

warnings: Boiling does not remove chemicals, fuel, or toxins. If the notice says 'do not drink' or 'do not use,' boiling will not make the water safe.
Never mix bleach with ammonia or other cleaners when disinfecting containers or dishes.
Let boiled water cool before handling or giving it to children to prevent scald burns.
Do not use water from a hot water heater for drinking if the tank sat in floodwater.
proTips: Keep a written card on the fridge: 1 minute rolling boil; 8 drops of 6% bleach per gallon, wait 30 minutes.
A large stockpot of boiled water each morning covers drinking and cooking for a family for the day.
Store at least 2 weeks of water so a short notice is an inconvenience, not an emergency.
Mark containers with the date you filled them and rotate stored water every 6 months.
whenNotTo: Do not boil water under a 'do not drink' or 'do not use' notice for chemical contamination - use bottled or stored water.
Do not use bleach on water that may contain fuel, chemicals, or floodwater from industrial areas - it will not make it safe.

quickGlance.situation: Your water utility issued a boil-water notice or the tap water has stopped.
immediate: Read the exact notice: boil vs. 'do not drink'
Boil 1 minute at a rolling boil (3 minutes at high altitude)
Use safe water for drinking, cooking, ice, teeth, and formula
then: No way to boil: 8 drops of 6% unscented bleach per gallon, wait 30 minutes
After the lift: flush taps, dump ice, replace filters

title: Dirty Bomb vs. Nuclear Detonation - Differences and Response
summary: How a radiological 'dirty bomb' differs from a nuclear explosion in size, danger, and response, why the first action is the same for both, and where the advice splits.

steps.title: Know what a dirty bomb is
steps.body: A dirty bomb, or radiological dispersal device (RDD), is ordinary explosives packed with radioactive powder or pellets. CDC stresses that it cannot cause a nuclear blast. The main danger is the explosion itself and flying debris. Only people very close to the blast are likely to get enough radiation to cause immediate serious illness. The bigger concern is radioactive dust and smoke drifting farther than the blast, which is harmful if people breathe it in or swallow it on food or in water. The affected area is far smaller than a nuclear explosion's, though cleanup can be long and costly.

steps.title: Know what a nuclear detonation is
steps.body: A nuclear detonation, including an improvised nuclear device (IND), is a true nuclear explosion. It creates a blinding flash, intense heat, a powerful blast wave that can destroy buildings over a wide area, and radioactive fallout that can travel many miles downwind. CDC notes it may also create an electromagnetic pulse that disrupts electronics. Fallout is the main threat to people who survive the blast, and the risk is highest in the first hours. Even a small device affects a far larger area than a dirty bomb.

steps.title: Do the same first thing for both: get inside
steps.body: CDC's core advice for both events is the same: get inside, stay inside, and stay tuned. You may not know at first which one happened. Get into the nearest sturdy building, ideally brick or concrete, and move to the basement or the middle of the building away from outer walls and the roof. Close windows and doors and turn off fans, air conditioning, and forced-air heat that pull in outside air. Do not go out to collect family members; schools and workplaces have shelter plans.

steps.title: Remove contamination from your body
steps.body: For either event, if you were outside, take off your outer layer of clothing as soon as you can; CDC says this can remove up to 90% of radioactive material. Seal the clothes in a plastic bag and put them away from people. Wash exposed skin and hair with soap and water, or wipe with a damp cloth. Do not scrub hard or scratch the skin. Put on clean clothes. Blow your nose and wipe your eyelids and ears gently. If you were hurt by blast debris, get medical care; injuries come first, and responders can treat contaminated patients safely.

steps.title: Where the advice splits: time and distance
steps.body: After a dirty bomb, the main goal is to avoid breathing dust. The affected zone is smaller, so officials may be able to clear many areas sooner; still wait for their instructions. If you are outside near a dirty bomb, cover your nose and mouth and get into the nearest sturdy building, moving away from the smoke and dust cloud if you can. After a nuclear detonation, fallout can arrive within minutes, so get inside at once rather than travel, and plan to stay inside at least 24 hours unless officials say otherwise. Fallout makes going outside early far more dangerous.

steps.title: Where the advice splits: potassium iodide
steps.body: Potassium iodide (KI) only protects the thyroid from radioactive iodine. FDA states that KI does not protect against radiation from a dirty bomb, which may contain other radioactive materials. After a nuclear detonation or a nuclear power plant accident, radioactive iodine may be released, and officials may tell some people to take KI. Take it only if public health officials tell you to, and follow the package label. Never use iodine antiseptic or iodized salt as a substitute.

steps.title: Stay tuned and follow officials
steps.body: Responders will measure radiation and announce which areas are safe, when to leave, and where to go for screening. Listen to a battery or hand-crank radio, TV, or phone alerts. Expect instructions about food and water, and do not eat garden produce or drink from open outdoor sources in the affected area until officials clear them. Sealed food and water inside buildings are generally safe. Many people may want to be checked for contamination; follow the location and timing officials give rather than rushing to emergency rooms if you are not hurt.

warnings: Do not take potassium iodide for a dirty bomb unless officials specifically tell you to - it will not protect you from most dirty-bomb materials.
Do not leave shelter early after a nuclear detonation to look for family. Fallout is deadliest in the first hours.
Do not pick up or keep any metal pieces, pellets, or debris near a blast site; they may be radioactive. Report them to police.
Cloth masks help against dust but do not stop radiation from fallout around you - shelter is what protects you.
proTips: If unsure which event happened, follow the stricter nuclear detonation steps until officials say otherwise.
Keep a bag with a change of clothes, soap, wet wipes, and plastic bags at work and in the car for quick decontamination.
A battery radio in your kit is the key tool, since officials will announce the exact zones to avoid.
Write 'Get Inside, Stay Inside, Stay Tuned' on your family plan card so kids remember it.

Frequently Asked Questions on Potassium Iodide (KI)

whenNotTo: Do not stay inside a building that is on fire or structurally damaged after the blast - move to another sturdy building.
Do not delay care for serious injuries to decontaminate first - get help for bleeding and breathing problems immediately.

quickGlance.situation: An explosion may have spread radioactive material, and you are not sure if it was a dirty bomb or a nuclear device.
immediate: Get inside a sturdy building now; go to the basement or center
Remove outer clothing, bag it, wash exposed skin
Close windows and doors; turn off outside air
then: Listen to officials for which event it was and when to leave
Take KI only if officials say to - it does not help for most dirty bombs

title: Returning Home Safely After a Disaster - Structure, Gas, Power, Mold, and Wildlife
summary: A step-by-step check for going back into your home after a flood, storm, fire, or earthquake: when it is safe to enter, how to handle gas and electrical hazards, how to clean up mold, and how to avoid animals and other hidden dangers.

steps.title: Wait for the all-clear and go in daylight
steps.body: Return only after local officials say your area is safe. Go during daylight so you can see hazards without needing to turn on power. Bring a battery flashlight (never candles or gas lanterns), a charged phone, water, a first aid kit, sturdy boots, heavy gloves, long pants, and an N95 respirator. Expect no power, water, sewer, or trash service. Do not bring children or pets on the first visit. Tell someone where you are going and when you expect to be back.

steps.title: Check the outside before you enter
steps.body: Walk all the way around the house first. Stay far away from downed power lines and anything touching them; assume they are live. CDC says not to enter if you see obvious damage such as cracks in walls or the foundation, a shifted or sagging roof, or trees on the house; have a building inspector or professional check it first. Look for a leaning chimney, broken gas lines, and standing water near the electric meter. If doors stick at the top, the frame may have shifted. When in doubt, stay out.

steps.title: Smell for gas
steps.body: If you smell gas (a rotten-egg odor) or hear hissing, CDC says to turn off the main gas valve if you can do so safely, open windows, leave the house right away, and call the gas company or fire department from outside. Do not turn on lights, use a phone, light anything, or do anything that could cause a spark while inside. Do not go back in until the gas company or fire department says it is safe. If you shut off the gas, only the utility or a licensed professional should turn it back on and relight pilot lights.

steps.title: Treat electricity as dangerous
steps.body: If there is standing water, turn off the main power only if you can reach the breaker box from a dry spot. If you would have to step into water to reach it, call an electrician. Never touch switches, plugs, or appliances while standing in water or with wet hands. Have an electrician inspect the system before power is turned back on after flooding. Appliances that got wet must dry completely and be checked before use. Never run a generator inside or within 20 feet (6 m) of any door, window, or vent, and use a battery CO alarm whenever fuel-burning equipment is running.

steps.title: Watch for animals and hidden hazards
steps.body: Floods, fires, and storms push snakes, rodents, raccoons, stray dogs, and stinging insects into homes and debris piles. Wear boots and gloves, look before you reach into dark spaces, and use a stick to move debris. Back away from any wild or stray animal and call animal control; do not try to catch it. Watch for nails, broken glass, and weak floors. If you are bitten or scratched by an animal, wash the wound with soap and water and get medical care promptly. Throw out food that touched floodwater or may have warmed during the outage.

steps.title: Document, then dry out fast
steps.body: Before cleaning, take photos and video of damage and belongings for insurance, then call your insurer. Open doors and windows and air the home out for at least 30 minutes before staying inside. CDC says to assume mold is present if the home was flooded and closed up for several days. Remove standing water and start drying right away with fans and dehumidifiers once power is safe. Throw away soaked carpet, mattresses, upholstered furniture, stuffed toys, and drywall or insulation that got wet, since mold grows into these and is hard to remove.

steps.title: Clean mold safely
steps.body: Wear an N95 respirator, goggles, and gloves while cleaning. EPA says homeowners can usually handle a moldy area smaller than about 10 square feet (roughly 3 feet by 3 feet); larger areas or sewage-contaminated water call for a professional. Scrub hard surfaces with detergent and water, or with a bleach solution of no more than 1 cup of bleach per gallon of water, then dry completely. Never mix bleach with ammonia or other cleaners. Do not paint or caulk over mold. Do not run a heating or cooling system that may be contaminated until it is cleaned.

warnings: Never enter a home with structural damage, a gas smell, or standing water near electrical equipment until a professional clears it.
Generators and pressure washers must run outdoors, at least 20 feet from openings - CO poisoning spikes during cleanup.
Never mix bleach with ammonia or other cleaning products; the fumes are toxic.
Floodwater can carry sewage and chemicals. Wash skin that touches it with soap and clean water, and keep cuts covered.
proTips: Pace yourself: drink water, take breaks, and accept help. Cleanup injuries often come from exhaustion.
Make a quick inventory video of every room each year so insurance claims are easier after a disaster.
Call or text 211 for local recovery resources, and the Disaster Distress Helpline at 1-800-985-5990 if stress becomes overwhelming.
Know where your gas shutoff valve is and keep the right wrench next to it before you ever need it.

sources.title: Safety Guidelines: Returning Home After a Natural Disaster
Safety Guidelines: Reentering Your Flooded Home

whenNotTo: Do not return before officials lift evacuation orders, even if your street looks fine.
Do not tackle large mold areas (over about 10 square feet) or sewage-soaked materials yourself if you have asthma, a weak immune system, or other health concerns - hire a professional.

quickGlance.situation: Officials say you can return home after a flood, storm, fire, or earthquake.
immediate: Go in daylight with a flashlight, boots, gloves, and an N95
Walk around outside first; stay out if there are cracks, sagging, or downed lines
Smell gas? Shut the main valve if safe, open windows, leave, call from outside
then: Shut off power from a dry spot only; have an electrician check before restoring
Photograph damage, air out 30 minutes, remove wet porous items, clean mold safely

title: Civil Unrest - Staying Safe Near Riots, Looting, and Breakdown
summary: How to keep your household safe when protests turn violent, looting starts, or a long disaster strains public order: stay away, stay informed, keep a low profile, and know when to leave.

steps.title: Avoid the area and stay indoors
steps.body: The safest choice is distance. Local emergency managers advise staying indoors and away from large crowds when unrest starts. Do not go to watch, film, or 'help' unless you are trained and assigned. Crowds can turn fast, and police may use barriers, chemical irritants, or mass arrests that sweep up bystanders. If you are caught near trouble, walk away calmly along side streets, keep a wall or building at your back, and do not run in a way that draws attention. Stay out of arguments with demonstrators, counter-protesters, or police.

steps.title: Get reliable information
steps.body: Follow your city or county emergency management agency, police, and local news, and sign up for local text alerts. Rumors spread fast during unrest and lead to bad choices, so check two trusted sources before acting. Learn the exact boundaries and hours of any curfew and obey it; violating one can get you arrested and makes you harder to tell apart from people causing harm. Keep a battery radio in case power or cell service fails. Share only confirmed information with your neighbors and family group.

steps.title: Secure and quiet your home
steps.body: Lock doors and windows and bring in items from the yard that could be stolen or thrown. On lower floors, close blinds and curtains so people outside cannot see in. Keep a low profile: do not display generators, fuel, food, or valuables, and avoid posting on social media about your supplies or that you are away. Park vehicles in a garage or out of sight if you can. Keep shoes, a flashlight, keys, phone, and a go-bag by the bed. Have a fire extinguisher ready; arson is a common danger during riots. Agree on a safe interior room for the family.

steps.title: Plan routes and travel carefully
steps.body: Roads may be blocked by crowds, police lines, or debris. Plan at least two alternate routes to work, school, and family, and keep at least half a tank of fuel. If you must drive, keep doors locked and windows up and leave space ahead so you can turn away. If a crowd surrounds your car, do not drive into people; stay calm, call 911, and leave when a path opens. Travel in daylight when possible. Tell someone your route and expected arrival time.

steps.title: Decide when to stay and when to go
steps.body: Staying home is usually safer when unrest is in another part of town and you have water, food, and medicine for several days. Leave early, before crowds and roadblocks form, if officials tell you to evacuate, if fire is spreading toward you, or if your building is being targeted. Go to family, friends, or an official shelter outside the affected area. Take your go-bag, medications, documents, phone charger, and pets. Lock up and leave no note on the door that shows you are gone. Let your out-of-area contact know where you went.

steps.title: Work with neighbors
steps.body: Neighbors who know and look out for each other are safer than any single household. Share phone numbers or a group chat, agree on how to warn each other, and check on older or disabled residents. Report crimes in progress to 911 and leave enforcement to police. In a long disaster where services are slow to return, pooling information, watching each other's homes, and sharing basics like water and medicine reduces desperation and conflict on your street.

steps.title: Know the law on force and property
steps.body: In most states you may not use deadly force just to protect property; it is generally limited to an immediate threat of death or serious injury to people. Laws vary widely by state, and a declared emergency usually does not change them. If anyone in your home owns firearms, store them locked and unloaded when not under direct control, and never brandish one to scare people away; that can be a crime and can escalate the situation. Your goal is to avoid any confrontation. Replace property later; you cannot replace people.

warnings: Deadly force to protect property alone is illegal in most states. Know your state's law before an emergency, and treat confrontation as the last resort.
Fires set during riots can spread to nearby homes. If smoke or fire approaches, leave early rather than wait.
Breaking curfew or entering police lines can lead to arrest or injury even if you mean no harm.
Do not rely on social media alone - false reports of violence or 'safe' routes are common during unrest.
proTips: Dress plainly and avoid clothing or patches that could be read as taking a side or as police or military gear.
Keep a small amount of cash and a printed list of key phone numbers in case card readers and phones go down.
If you get exposed to tear gas or pepper spray, move upwind to fresh air, remove contaminated outer clothing, and flush eyes and skin with lots of clean water.
Practice your 'leave in 10 minutes' drill: who grabs what, which car, which route.
source: Local emergency management guidance (Salt Lake County EM, NIST OEP)

sources.title: OEP Quick Reference Guide: Civil Disturbance

whenNotTo: Do not shelter in place if fire is spreading toward your home or officials order an evacuation.
Do not try to defend a business or property against a crowd - leave and let police handle it.

quickGlance.situation: Riots, looting, or violent protests are happening in or near your area.
immediate: Stay indoors and away from crowds; do not go to watch
Lock up, close lower-floor blinds, keep a low profile
Follow official alerts and obey any curfew
Call 911 for violence or threats - do not confront
then: Plan two alternate routes and keep the car fueled
Leave early if fire approaches, officials order it, or your building is targeted
